subsubtopic: EFFECT OF HIGH INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday the central bank lending rate rose again, increasing to intolerable levels the financial pressure on the ordinary citizens of our country. In view of the fact that high interest rates have made construction of new apartment buildings and homes an unviable proposition, and that my city of Edmonton presently has a vacancy rate of only 1.1 per cent, with many people there facing mortgage renewals, rental increases and loss of income through increasing lay-offs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That the Minister of Finance take immediate steps to reduce present high interest rates, which are severely damaging not only the economy, but the lives of hard-working Canadians desperately worried about their own future.

Canadians cannot honestly expect farmers to continue to produce grain at prices lower than last year when the farm input price index in western Canada skyrocketed by 11.2 per cent during that time. That this House calls upon the minister responsible for the Wheat Board to show the courage and leadership which his office demands and immediately raise the initial prices to a realistic level which will allow farmers to cover the payments on their input costs which will come due this fall.

AWARDING OF MEGAPROJECT CONTRACTS TO FOREIGN FIRMS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on the matter of jobs from energy megaprojects. First we had the stacker reclaimer case in Prince Rupert and now we have a similar situation in the coal project at Sparwood, British Columbia. I have just been informed by letter from the regional manager of Westeel-Rosco Limited in Vancouver that a S20 million contract for conveyor covers was awarded to Continental Conveyor and Equipment of Alabama Inc., U.S.A. The American company gave assurances that almost all the components would be made in Canada. Continental then promptly awarded the work to a Chicago-based company and Canada lost another 20,000 manhours of work. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That in order that the highly touted spin-off effect of Canadian energy megaprojects does not rapidly turn into a tailspin, the Government of Canada take immediate concrete steps so that Canadian resources can be used to help Canadian business and governments to provide jobs for Canadians and not allow them to go out of the country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity to seek the unanimous consent of the House. Soviet Jewish dissident Anatoly Shcharansky has been unjustly held for over six months in solitary confinement and on low rations by the Soviet authorities, in direct contravention of basic human rights and of Soviet obligations under the Helsinki Accord to respect the fundamental freedoms of conscience and religion. In view of this injustice and the plea of Mr. Shcharansky's wife that politicians in the west take up her husband's cause, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith):
That this House call on the Soviet Union to live up to its obligation under the Helsinki Accord and immediately release Anatoly Shcharansky from detention.

subsubtopic: TAXES ON GASOLINE AND DIESEL FUEL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are paying more in taxes than they do for food and shelter. Many of these taxes are hidden in consumer goods such as gasoline where, in spite of falling world prices, Canadians pay an increasing amount of hidden taxes which are justified by such things as the need to raise prices to world levels and the need to pay for oil imports even while available Canadian oil is not being used. As an example, Ontario farmers who use
gasoline are relieved from federal excise and sales tax of 20 cents a gallon while they are still paying 40 cents a gallon for other federal taxes. Ontario motorists now pay over 60 cents a gallon combined federal tax, and the federal government claims the largest single bite on a gallon of gas, 34.5 per cent. If the federal government is serious about fighting inflation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger):
That the federal government immediately reduce the crushing burden of gasoline and diesel fuel taxation to consumers, and implement a rebate program on gasoline and diesel fuel to agricultural producers.

subsubtopic: MONETARY POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister. We all know that the chartered banks raised their prime lending rate to 17 per cent yesterday. We expect this to be a trend going into the spring and summer months. It seems that our high interest rate policy will be with us for a while. Mr. Bouey says that there will not be any change in the monetary policy. We have had this type of policy since 1975, and in terms of fighting inflation it has not worked. It obviously has not worked because our inflation rate is much higher now than it was in 1975.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister how much longer he expects we will have to wait for this to take effect? At what point will he change the monetary policy that we have now, as it obviously is not working?

I suggest to him the answer that was given by Governor Bouey to the finance committee yesterday, that the real cure to the interest rate problems we are facing is a severe and sustained attack on inflation. Madam Speaker, you will remember that yesterday afternoon in the House I asked a very specific question of the Prime Minister relating to any drastic change in government policy respecting gambling or off-track betting. The Prime Minister left the very distinct impression-and I would suggest that he intended to leave that very distinct impression with the House-that he knew nothing about any change in policy, that no change in policy would be effected by order in council, regulation or in any such way and, furthermore, if there was a change in policy forthcoming that it would be by legislative amendment to the Criminal Code, with all of which I agreed.
At approximately 5.30 last night, three hours after that exchange in the House, a press release was received in the press gallery, in the name of the absentee Minister of Agriculture, indicating that indeed by some form of ministerial regulation or departmental regulation a drastic change in regard to government policy on such a controversial issue as off-track betting had taken place. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

Madam Speaker, the hon. member will recall that when he asked me the question my first answer was to say that I would take notice of it, that I was not aware of any impending change of the nature about which the hon. member asked, to wit, a change by order in council. There has been a change by governmental regulation, by departmental regulation, which is something authorized under the law to which the hon. member referred.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, March 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-97, to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, and to provide for payments to certain provinces, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I wish to continue the debate on Bill C-97, an act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977 and to provide for payments to certain provinces. This bill has caused considerable controversy across the country. It has become one of the most important bills to be debated so far this session.
I wish to refer to a Conservative task force which travelled across the country earlier this year dealing with the budget and transfer payments. The document is entitled "They didn't ask us!". This seems to be a main problem with this government; it is acting unilaterally and not properly consulting the provinces, individuals, businesses or whatever.
1 wish to comment on a few of the statements by individuals and organizations which the Conservative committee met while travelling across the country. Some of these statements regarding federal programs were made by the City of Saint John, which stated:
The elimination of federal programs which were designed to help municipal governments was a very serious blow to the kinds of services which citizens require at local levels.
The elimination of this type of grant to the provinces and cities will cause more lay-offs. If there was proper funding, there would be more hiring. The municipalities would do a lot of their local work. The Students' Union of Nova Scotia in Halifax stated:
-post-secondary education in Nova Scotia will suffer as a result of the budget.
The government did not communicate with these groups prior to the cutbacks. Dr. Howard Dixon, Professor of Anatomy, Dalhousie University, Halifax, stated:
Clinical research faces the prospect of receiving a doubly severe blow from Mr. MacEachen's budget-not only will it be hampered by university cuts, but also by the increased financial burdens placed on hospitals as well.
Nobody has escaped the budget, the fiscal arrangements with the provinces and the cutbacks. The Saint John Construction Association in Saint John, New Brunswick, stated to our Conservative committee:
Mobility taxes will encourage workers to stay where they are and collect UIC.
That could cause another very serious problem. Dalhousie Bio-medical Research in Halifax stated:
March 26, 1982

The removal of billions will surely grease the skids for an accelerated decline of the university system as we know it.
We made a number of recommendations. I just want to name some of them. We found out from our communications and meeting with universities, individuals and businesses that what we need in this country is to, and I quote:
Restore individual and investor confidence by establishing a climate for growth, development and expansion.
Most of the witnesses who appeared before the committee said the government should, and I quote:
Withdraw the November 12 budget and replace it with an economic plan that will promote job-creation and economic development through private investment.
One of the highlights of the committee's conclusions and recommendations was that we should:
Restore harmonious federal-provincial relationships and ensure adequate federal funding of provincial health, education and other important ... programs.
I am going to go into that subject in a little more detail.
Newspapers, individuals and the provinces have all been expressing opinions on these transfer payments. We get a different story from each individual and each newspaper. One matter that will have to be gone into very thoroughly when it gets to the standing committee is who was right and who was wrong with regard to the amounts being cut back and the amounts going to the different provinces.
Earlier this week the Montreal Gazette's Ottawa bureau expressed its opinion on the budget in an article headlined "Ottawa to transfer $1.4 billion more to Quebec". I do not know the reason one province will receive an additional $1.4 billion to that which was first announced in November. According to the Montreal Gazette, four months later we find that an additional $1.4 billion will be paid to the province of Quebec. I quote from the article:
During the same five years, 1982 to 1987, yesterday's bill would cut by $405 million the equalization handouts to Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
The contents of this news article will have to be studied in detail by the committee. I again quote from the article:
In Halifax, Nova Scotia finance minister Joe Matheson said he hadn't expected the new bill to do so much for Quebec, but reserved further comment until he sees the Ottawa legislation.
1 hope that matter can be cleared up. If an additional $1.4 billion is going to the province of Quebec, other provinces in Canada deserve a detailed explanation why. Also, an assessment by the Toronto Star states:
Ontario, for example, stands to see $1.9 billion cut from federal contributions to health care and university funding over the next five years. As Ontario's deputy treasurer, Mr. Campbell, points out, the reductions will cut deeply into programs that the federal government itself encouraged the provinces to establish and build up over the past decade.
So we see reports of $ 1.4 billion more for one province and $1.9 billion less for another province.
We have also seen statements from the Manitoba government about how federal cutbacks will hurt that province the most. I do not know why Manitoba has been singled out to be
Federal Transfers to Provinces
hurt the most but apparently this has been decided by the Liberal government.
As a result of the new federal proposals to cut back on transfer payments, Manitoba stands to lose significantly more per capita than any other province. It was pointed out in the recent federal-provincial finance ministers' meeting in Ottawa that planned changes in the federal equalization payments and shared cost programs for health, medicare and post-secondary education should not be made until the full implementation of the proposals are known and a general consensus reached with the provinces. There are considerably detailed reports from Manitoba which indicate exactly where we will be hurt.
We want to know why the province of Quebec will receive an additional $1.4 billion, especially considering the way it runs its financial affairs. I suggest that there should be a moratorium on federal funding to Quebec until we find out exactly what its debt is, since there are rumours that it will reach $9 billion.
We have received many figures from the Department of Finance on transfer payments and other related items. Since these figures are not entirely clear, the committee will have to do a great deal of work in order to prepare detailed explanations to each province, as well as the House, with regard to these transfer payments.
The cutback in health care payments to provinces is of major concern to Canadians and we must attempt to maintain the standards which were established by the Conservative Party with regard to health care which date back to 1938. The Right Hon. Mr. Diefenbaker pointed out at that time that free hospitalization and medicare for the people of Saskatchewan was a number one priority for the Conservative Party. Mr Diefenbaker pointed out that the Progressive Conservative Party believed that the removal of deterrent fees for prescription drugs would increase the number of drugs provided under the plan. This position which was taken in 1938 at a Conservative convention in the province of Saskatchewan was the beginning of major health care programs in Canada.
During the last two federal elections there have been problems caused by Liberal and New Democratic Party candidates misinforming the electorate with regard to what was happening with health care payments provided to the provinces by the federal government. I have to combat these problems extensively when the Liberals and New Democrats misled and misinformed the people at every turn during the last two campaigns by stating that the province of Manitoba, which had a Conservative government at that time, was using federally provided health care funds to build roads. Of course, that statement was completely false. The Liberals have commenced their last two compaigns in Manitoba with this blatant lie. Of course, they had the full support of their NDP cohorts.
In 1979, the Conservative government commissioned Mr. Emmett Hall to do a study called "Canada's National-Provincial Program for the 1980s". After conducting a thorough investigation into how the funds were distributed for health care in Manitoba, Mr. Hall stated:

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
I conclude therefore that the first part of the allegation, namely that "federal health dollars are being diverted", is not established.
He found absolutely no proof that the funds were being diverted to build highways and the NDP and the Liberals had absolutely no evidence of this. They were completely misleading and misinforming the public. No doubt they were using the same tactics in other provinces.
I can illustrate what a commendable job the Lyon government did for health care in Manitoba by referring to the 197778 budget which was brought in by the NDP government at that time. The NDP government was only increasing funding for health care by 0.1 per cent and consequently the percentage allocated to health care under the Lyon government which followed them rose from 34 per cent to 36 per cent. This placed Manitoba second only to British Columbia in the proportion of funds allocated to health care. This was accomplished by the Lyon Conservative government during their tenure. They had a much more commendable record for increasing health care funding than the previous NDP government.
There still has to be some investigation into the allocation of funds in health care, particularly in the province of Saskatchewan where there is a continual problem with regard to the amount being spent in that area. Before 1 deal with those figures, I will read some comments made by the former leader of the NDP, Mr. Tommy Douglas, when he wrote an article about medicare. He stated:
There are two of his-
He was referring to Mr. Diefenbaker's accomplishments.
-accomplishments which 1 shall always remember with gratitude and for which Canada owed him a great deal. When he became Prime Minister he amended the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to provide that Ottawa would pay approximately half the cost of hospital care in any province willing to provide such service. And he set up a royal commission under the Chairmanship of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall on comprehensive health insurance which was implemented in 1968 and constituted a major step towards comprehensive health insurance for all Canadians.
We want to maintain these standards which were originally established by Conservative governments. We do not want to see them deteriorate, as they are in the province of Saskatchewan. Due to the refusal of the Government of Saskatchewan to increase doctors' fees to a reasonable level, some patients must now pay for medical services received. After forwarding bills to the medicare commission, Saskatchewan citizens may discover that they are eligible for only a partial reimbursement, in some cases as little as 50 per cent.
Statistics from British Columbia to Quebec illustrate the position of the Saskatchewan government in relation to other provincial governments on per capita medical expenditures. These statistics show that Saskatchewan has the lowest expenditure. These figures speak for themselves. The per capita expenditure in British Columbia is $555; in Alberta $548; in Saskatchewan $534; in Manitoba $639, which is much higher than what is being spent in the NDP province of Saskatchewan; Ontario spends $547 per capita and Quebec spends $647.
There have been other problems with health care in Saskatchewan as well. The minister of health of that province has
stated to doctors in the past that he wants to discourage return visits. We have to be very careful about health ministers getting into the medical business and telling practitioners when patients should come for second or third visits. The Saskatchewan health minister stated physicians should be:
-telling patients who are in the office frequently, say every two or three weeks, that their problem "might not be medical";-
That is not a decision for anybody in the NDP government in Saskatchewan to make. That is entirely up to physicians. I suggest the Saskatchewan health minister keep his nose out of the medical practitioner business and let medical practitioners judge when patients should come to their offices.
I have recognized this problem in Saskatchewan for some time. In 1979 I introduced a motion in the House regarding a reduction of contributions to health care in the province of Saskatchewan. I said:
In view of the fact that since the time medicare was instituted in Saskatchewan, many doctors traditionally have not participated in the medicare plan, that 30 per cent of doctors in that province now are billing patients directly, that less than 5 per cent of doctors in Manitoba are operating outside the plan, and that there is a significant decrease in the budget for hospital insurance and medicare programs in Saskatchewan, I move ...
That the Minister of National Health and Welfare advise the recently appointed Hall commission to study immediately the reasons for the deteriorating budgetary contributions by the Saskatchewan NDP government for medicare, as well as the significant increase of extra billing by doctors in Saskatchewan.
I received support from my colleagues in the Conservative Party. I received support at that time from the members of the Liberal Party. The "Noes" came from the New Democratic Party. Hon. members in the New Democratic Party were frightened to death to have an investigation into deteriorating health services in the province of Saskatchewan.
In closing, I would like to talk about how we could increase funding to the provinces. I recommend that the Liberal government stop making special low-interest loans to Communist countries. The Liberal Party has lined up a special deal for the Russian communist government. A loan of $637 million has been arranged. The money is being borrowed in Canada at 16 per cent and lent over a repayment period of 12 years at an interest rate of 10 per cent to the Communists. The result would be a Canadian subsidy of $198.5 million in terms of future dollars or $139 million in present dollars. That money could be put to better use in Canada. It could provide low-interest loans to the provinces or individuals for housing. We should not be looking after communist countries. Let them look after themselves.
Another flagrant example of misuse of Canadian funds is the fact that we are helping to build a monument in Algiers. In that country the EDC portion of a $97.8 million loan is part of a $1.2 billion line of credit negotiated between Canada and Algeria in 1978 and expiring at the end of 1982. The Algerians get the EDC funds at somewhat less than 11 per cent interest, the rates prevailing in 1978, yet the Crown body must borrow at between 16 per cent and 17 per cent today. Someone-the
March 26, 1982

Canadian taxpayer-is making up the difference for this. I think it is time the Liberal government took a serious look at these types of subsidized loans to other countries. The information I have is that we receive very few benefits from these huge subsidized loans.
As I said earlier, the standing committee will have its work cut out for it in dealing with transfer payments. There should be an explanation especially as to why Manitoba's funding has been reduced so much and why we are getting reports of an additional $1.4 billion going to the province of Quebec. I will be calling on members of the committee not only from the government side but also from our side to make sure we get a detailed explanation of which provinces are getting what. This confusion should be cleared up once and for all.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate because of the importance of the subject. Difficulties will be created for our health care system and our postsecondary education as a result of the proposals brought forward by the government in this bill. I also enter the debate because I am one of the members who was here in 1972 and in 1977 when this same Liberal government brought forward proposals which began the process of cutting back. The process will eventually destroy the health care system and the postsecondary education system we have had since the end of World War II.
What we are being asked to do if we pass this bill is to take another step in the direction set in 1972 and accelerated in 1977 toward the destruction of a health care system and a post-secondary education system which has been national in scope and has provided services in the fields of hospital care, medical care and university education. We have a fairly equitable system serving all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific at a certain basic standard.
This was not always the case. Many Canadians and many Members of Parliament cannot remember the time, because they are fairly young, when they or their neighbours could not see a doctor or enter a hospital because they simply could not afford to pay for those services. There was no universal government insurance which paid the bills incurred for hospital or medical services until the mid-1940s. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) quoted a former leader of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Douglas, who paid tribute to the contribution made by a former Conservative prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker. It was a CCF government headed by Mr. Douglas which, in the 1940s, first inaugurated a non-profit hospital insurance plan which paid the hospital bills of all the residents of Saskatchewan who entered hospital. It was a federal Conservative government headed by Mr. Diefenbaker which passed legislation requiring the federal government to pay half the cost of a similar plan in any province in the country. That brought the other provinces into hospital insurance and eliminated the fear of bankruptcy many Canadians faced before hospital insurance was brought in. This prospect still faces many citizens of the United States if they have prolonged illnesses, because they have no hospital insurance plan such as ours.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
It was the same Conservative government headed by Mr. Diefenbaker which appointed Mr. Justice Hall to head a royal commission to study medical care. The report of that commission headed by Mr. Hall was brought down at a time when we had a Liberal government headed by Mr. Pearson, and that report led to the proposal by the then Liberal government offering the provinces financial inducements which led them to follow the example of the Saskatchewan CCF government respecting a universal medical insurance plan in each province which pays the fees for medical services provided by doctors. That plan came to fruition because the Liberal government agreed to pay 50 per cent of the cost of medical insurance plans. The Conservative province of Ontario was the last one to join in the medical insurance plan. It was brought in kicking and screaming because it did not like the plan. It still believed that the earlier non-profit, voluntary plans were better even though they excluded about 30 per cent of the people who could not afford to pay the premiums. But it could not stay out of the new plan because the people of Ontario, like those of every other province, recognized the benefits which would accrue to them.
There were some variations in the methods of financing. Some provinces finance the cost of medical insurance out of general revenue and some, like Ontario and British Columbia, require citizens to pay premiums. With these variations in the method of financing, the plans have worked quite well. They could be improved, of course, but until recently they met the basic needs of Canadian citizens.
In recent years costs have gone up for both federal and provincial governments. While that is true, the percentage of the GNP which the provinces and the federal government pay for health care has not gone up. Both the federal and provincial governments are finding it difficult to finance all the services they provide. This is partly due to the fact that the economy is not working at anything like full capacity. Revenues of the federal and provincial governments have decreased and they have begun to argue that they cannot afford the plans that are in place. They have taken steps which will result in destroying the universality and availability of the basic medical and hospital services provided for all Canadians.
Some provinces have instituted deterrent fees for hospital stays and doctor visits. This makes things difficult for senior citizens, the one million unemployed and the working poor. There is more and more extra billing by doctors because the provinces claim that they simply cannot afford to give doctors the high incomes they desire.
Canadians are fairly critical of doctors, Mr. Speaker. According to Statistics Canada they have the highest income of any group. We must face the fact, however, that their incomes have not increased in recent years as much as the cost of living has, so in effect they have suffered a reduction in real income.
In 1977 the Liberal government began to whittle at the system of health care which it had played a major role in

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
establishing. In that year it replaced the 50-50 cost-sharing arrangement with a block grant system under which the provinces were not required to match federal grants for health care, hospital insurance or post-secondary education, as had been the case until then. They put the cap on the federal contribution to those programs.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, who spoke ahead of me in this debate, tried to indicate that the provinces had not cut back on their expenditures on health care and hospital insurance. Of course they had, Mr. Speaker. They did so because once they were not required to pay 50 per cent of the cost of hospital insurance, health care or post-secondary education, they used the block fund grant from the federal government for other purposes. They were entitled to do that under the new agreement made with the Liberal government in 1977.
At that time members of the New Democratic Party in this House warned that this would lead to a fragmentation of the system and that the have-not provinces would not be able to match the programs offered by the wealthy provinces. That is what has happened. Provinces such as New Brunswick have imposed deterrent fees because they simply cannot afford to carry the cost of the services. Most of us did not foresee that the provinces, particularly some of the Conservative provinces, would use the block funding as an excuse for not continuing to match federal grants. The provincial cost of these programs has fallen.
We should not be surprised at that. The revenues of seven of the ten provinces are in bad shape because we are in a period of economic recession which has been brought about to a large extent by the mistaken policies of the Liberal government, aided and abetted by the mistaken high interest rate policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. He seems to be determined to continue those policies even though, in the six or seven years they have been followed, unemployment has increased drastically, as has the rate of inflation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Governor of the Bank of Canada have been dead wrong but they seem determined to continue the mistaken policies they began six or seven years ago. The provinces are just doing what comes naturally to them; they are cutting back on funding of hospitals, medical insurance and post-secondary education. This is at a time when the federal government, in the bill we are now discussing, proposes to cut back on the agreement it forced on the provinces in 1977.
Let us keep the record clear, Mr. Speaker. It is not the established programs financing part of the 1977 fiscal arrangements act which is being changed. What we are changing with this bill is the equalization portion of the 1977 agreement, the purpose of which was to enable all the provinces to provide reasonable levels of public service.
The provinces used the block funding agreement to claim that the money received with the revenue guarantee was unconditional and that they were not required to match the federal grants for hospital, medical and post-secondary education.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine said, quite properly, that New Democratic Members of Parliament and members all across the country criticized the Conservative provincial governments for doing that. He said we were wrong. He should also have put on the record the criticisms of those governments by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) who has been attacking them for reduced spending on these programs and has threatened to take action. She has said, quite correctly, that that kind of reduction will lead to the destruction of the medical insurance program. She ought to make those arguments not to the provincial governments, and not out on the hustings, but to the Minister of Finance.
In his November budget the Minister of Finance argued, as the provinces had, that the money associated with the revenue guarantee "was never intended to finance health care and postsecondary education programs", even though in the cheques from the federal government to the provinces this money was always included.
Now, as a logical extension of the November budget, we have Bill C-97. It will put in place the mechanism to remove the revenue guarantee and will reduce federal contributions to the provinces in the next five years by $5.7 billion. This proposal has been attacked and criticized, naturally, by the provinces because they simply do not know how they will make up very drastic reductions in the moneys they were obtaining from the federal government. Also it was criticized very severely by the Economic Council of Canada. The Council warned that the cuts would inevitably lead to higher provincial taxes, to more user fees in health care and education, or to a reduction in services.
We have not had an explanation from the Minister of Finance or any other Liberal government spokesman as to how the provinces could avoid increasing their taxes to meet the shortfall which the federal government is forcing upon them, cutting services, or increasing fees for services which people in the provinces will have to pay if the services are not to be cut. It is not surprising that the provinces, especially the have-not ones, have come to the conclusion that the provisions of this bill, when implemented, will have a very detrimental effect upon them when, in the case of seven provinces, they are already facing very serious budgetary deficits.
Let me illustrate the problem faced by some provinces. In the province of Manitoba the government was left a deficit by the former Conservative government of close to $300 million when it took office. The new arrangement being forced upon the province by the Liberal government will mean a reduction in what it would have obtained under the 1977 agreement of over $60 million in 1982-83, $122 million in 1983-84, $172 million in 1984-85, $223 million in 1985-86, and $246 million in 1986-87. That is a five-year total of $828 million. There were some last minute negotiations between the province of Manitoba and the federal government, and that amount has
March 26, 1982

been reduced to S719 million, which is still a very substantial amount.
Let us look at another have-not province, the province of Nova Scotia. In the first year under the new agreement it will lose S28 million; in the second year, $32 million; in the third year, $36 million; in the fourth year, $41 million; in the fifth year, $46 million; for a total of over $183 million in five years. This is in a province which faces a budgetary deficit this year of close to $500 million.
If I heard the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine correctly, he seemed to imply that under the new agreement the province of Quebec will receive more money than it would have under the old agreement. In fact, in the next five years the province of Quebec will receive $1,363 million less under the new plan than it would have under the agreement which was reached in 1977. If we total the reduction in federal contributions under the new bill for all provinces and the territories, we see a reduction in the next five years of $5.7 billion. That is a scenario for disaster.
We are already seeing the results of restraint programs. There have been increases in user fees in British Columbia and Ontario, a reduction in ward bed numbers, increases in fees for semi-private rooms, and the opening up of commercial space in Ontario hospitals. If Ontario hospitals are permitted some free enterprise, and if they have big deficits, they will concentrate their efforts on semi-private and private rooms on which they will be able to charge whatever they can obtain. Of course, this will reduce the kind of service and the number of beds available to ordinary citizens of Ontario who cannot afford to pay for semi-private or private rooms.
Also we are seeing a substantial increase in the number of doctors who are extra billing. We are seeing threats, actual strikes, slowdowns or work to rule by doctors in different provinces. The universal equitable health care system, which we brought into being over a period of many years after World War II, is in danger of being broken, if not destroyed.
In rejecting the government's decision to cut back funding for existing programs, am I arguing that the present system is meeting all our needs? Not at all. We need to re-examine what we have accomplished. Changes are needed, improvements can be made. Some improvements might even save money by providing alternatives to the present expensive system which would cost less than present methods and provide better service.
Before making suggestions regarding some of the items at which we should be looking, I want to spend a few minutes discussing the problems of Canadian universities. I should like to give an historical perspective. Until the end of World War II we, in Canada, probably had only three or four universities which were of a standard achieved in other countries such as the United States, Great Britain and other western European countries. In 1946-47, the then Liberal government began to fund university education, partly because there were many veterans of World War II who wanted to attend university. In 1951, the then Liberal government began to give grants to the provinces for university education on a regular basis. By 1966, these grants had grown to almost $100 million for the year. In
Federal Transfers to Provinces
1967, the then Liberal prime minister, Mr. Pearson, argued that there was a broad national interest in maintaining a minimum level of services across the country in universities. He proposed a program under which the federal government would pay 50 per cent of the operating costs of Canadian universities in all parts of the country.
In 1972 the Liberal government put a cap on federal funding for post-secondary education, so that the annual increase of federal funds could not be more than 15 per cent in any one year. Under the 1972 act costs increased very rapidly. For education, federal funding rose from $1 billion in 1972-73 to $1.7 billion in 1976-77; it almost doubled. Hospital insurance funding by the federal government went to $2.6 billion in 1976-77, and medical insurance went to almost $1 billion, or $961 million, that year.
Let us give credit where credit is due. Without massive increases by the federal government in funding to Canadian universities and health care systems, we would have been in real difficulty by the late 1970s. They would have been very different from what in fact they are. In 1977 the legislation freed the federal government from having its expenditures tied directly to the cost of provincially-administered programs for health care and post-secondary education. The present proposal continues changes which began in 1977.
I have already indicated the serious effects that the proposal will have on the health care system, but what about universities? One hears stories or suggestions that universities are being too extravagant, that they are too rich, that we cannot afford them, and that they are not doing the job they ought to be doing. There is no truth to those suggestions, whether they come from federal government sources or from provincial governments. Let us look at the facts. In Manitoba this year the new NDP government has given the universities an increase of over 16 per cent. That is more than the increase in the cost of living. This will just begin to overcome the disastrous underfunding of four years of Conservative government in Manitoba. The reduction of funding in this bill will deal a body blow to Manitoban universities.
Let me put on the record the situation of the universities in Manitoba, and I will do it quite briefly. Brandon University is a small university located in the western part of our province. In the last four years, the library acquisition budget has increased by only $5,000. That is an example of the difficulties it is experiencing.
The University of Winnipeg, at which the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) taught before he came to this House, suffers one of the worst staff-student ratios in Canada, and faculty salaries which were edging up toward the national median have now crashed to the near bottom level. Research funds have scarecly increased in recent years. Library acquisitions have fallen sharply in recent years. According to library projections they will be cut in half in the next five years.
15868

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
At the University of Manitoba, which is the largest and most successful university in our province, students are using 40-year-old microscopes and 80-year-old rock samples. Money is lacking to buy new books and to hire teaching assistants. That is the situation in Manitoba. The proposal contained in this bill which will cut funding from the federal government substantially will have a disastrous effect on our universities.
What about the province of Ontario? In a study done for the provincial government, it was pointed out that the funding pattern that government has used has resulted in university operating grants falling almost 17 per cent in real dollars over the last ten years. A special committee appointed by the provincial government reported that without funding to match inflation, without additional funds to provide for faculty and staff advancement and without special funds to replace equipment and furniture, there would have to be an immediate move to restructure the system. Over four years government spending in Ontario has declined in real dollars adjusted for inflation by almost 5 per cent. University operating grants have declined by almost 13 per cent.
What will happen when the federal grants are cut as substantially as I have indicated, and as proposed in this legislation? Our universities and community colleges need more support from both levels of government, not less, if these universities and colleges are going to give us the trained, educated people to meet the challenges of the 1980s and 1990s in Canada. Almost every industrialized country in the western world spends more in terms of supporting universities and community colleges.
It is whispered by some in the federal government that our universities have been doing a poor job, that they have been training the wrong people for the wrong jobs. It has been suggested that Ottawa can do it better. This is a year in which we have well over one million unemployed and in which we are spending about $800 million on manpower training. This is a year when just a few days ago the Minister of Employment and Immigration made it clear that he would have to permit 20,000 to 25,000 skilled workers from offshore to enter Canada in order to meet our manpower shortage. How can a government which has failed so miserably to meet the need for skilled manpower, a field in which the government has almost complete control, suggest for a moment that it can do a better job of directing the universities to do what is needed than the universities have done up until now?
What we need is a co-operative effort by the federal government and the provinces, the educational institutions and the communities to rethink what we have accomplished, what our mistakes have been, what our needs are and what new programs we should implement. What we do not need but what we seem to be getting in this bill is the kind of unilateral action on the part of the federal government which has been such a disaster in the past.
Let me indicate a few of the problems which I think should be examined and make some tentative suggestions to deal with them. What the federal government is proposing in this bill is a
quick, surgical cut which fails to deal with real needs in the fields of education or health. The government does not deal with alternative methods of delivery which might very well do a better job and be cheaper. The federal government does not deal with preventive medicine. Both things are necessary. Alternatives in delivery would attempt to deal with relative ineffectiveness and escalating costs of searching for ways in which to improve performance at the same time as it would seek to lower costs. Preventive medicine is frequently talked about. Those in the field know how little has been done and how limited the provision of funds has been. They know they cannot do the job. We see evidence of that every day in reports of deaths and illness caused by not having cleaned up our environment and not providing for the kinds of safety measures required in our mines and factories.
Let me deal with some specific suggestions as to what we ought to do. Many people in Canada do not get the kind of health care they need. They do not get the kind of advice they need. They turn to the people they see every day, the people with whom they live, their peers, instead of turning to professional counsellors. They do that because they know these people but they do not understand them. Therefore, they cannot get the information they need.
We need to develop a training program for peers to deal with the disadvantaged group so that people can communicate. We have the beginnings of that kind of a training program right here in Ottawa at Algonquin College. We need to explore the possibility of developing a system for providing physicians' assistants. This kind of occupational group could bridge the gap between a medical doctor and a nurse. This is a very useful profession. It would be particularly useful in isolated communities in which it is difficult to get doctors to locate. This kind of program has begun already in Alaska.
We need to train more natives as nurses. This would encourage the natives to bring health services to their communities which are so often-

I was at the point of suggesting that a major effort should be made to encourage more native people to become nurses. It is unlikely in the foreseeable future that we can persuade enough of the people who have traditionally gone into the health care

field, either as doctors or nurses, to work in isolated areas near the reserves where so many of our native people live.
I believe real benefits would accrue if we could encourage more native people to become nurses. They could provide these services not only in a technical way, but they would have the knowledge and be able to communicate in the language and in light of the customs of the native people. Programs like these have been very successful in the city of Winnipeg and I would urge the minister to give consideration to beginning to expand those programs.
Mr. Speaker, we need to expand our communications networks so that we might deliver post-secondary education to individuals who live too far from present college campuses. These courses can now be packaged in many ways. For example, the instructor and student can be in contact by telephone as well as by television. This is being done now, I understand, on a very small scale in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. Some of the other provinces may Find it too expensive to develop on their own and it may be that the federal government can help.
We have seen an increasing incidence of racial prejudice and racial discrimination, as we have seen an increasing number of native people moving into our cities and an ever-increasing number of immigrants coming from non-English or nonFrench speaking countries to the cities of Canada. These people often find it difficult, if not impossible, to deal with those who work in our educational institutions and in our social services institutions to which they frequently used to call for help. We need to train people who can work with both our new and our old Canadians. This is a field where programs would pay dividends both financially and in meeting the needs of all people.
We have seen new problems arising in the field of mental health. With the development of the tranquillizer drugs, many people who earlier spent years, if not their whole lives, in mental hospitals have been and are being released. The idea was that they would be serviced outside in the community which would help them in the transition years. It has been reported a number of times in the last couple of weeks that even in a city like Toronto there are very few services for these people, so they are going back to the hospitals again. That problem needs to be dealt with.
We also need to deal with the increasing number of teenage pregnancies, child abuse and juvenile delinquency. We do not know enough about how to deal with these things, but we need to find new methods because the cost of not dealing with these problems is escalating very sharply. We have a whole host of disadvantaged people whose education stopped too soon and who do not fit into our increasingly technological, complicated society.
Our post-secondary education needs to make real strides. It has made real strides in the past decade, but now that these people can receive regular service, they often require extra

help in reading or in family support to compensate for earlier neglect. Unfortunately, in this time of Fiscal stress the minimum servicing we have provided up to now is being threatened.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the bill concerning Fiscal transfers and established programs Financing introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I believe this debate is important because it concerns a very important aspect of our federal system of government.
Mr. Speaker, we must realize that fiscal arrangements constitute a truly unique system. There is probably no other country in the world that has a system through which it can influence events occurring within the jurisdiction of another level of government. When there is a national program or national aspiration and the Parliament of Canada, even if the matter is not within its jurisdiction, decides to act in the interests of all Canadians and in the interest of fairness, a system such as Fiscal arrangements provides a mechanism for making use of the entire country's resources, without changing the constitutional order-and I would say that this last is extremely important. Both levels of government agree on an automatic payment system, and although at the present time there is some disagreement as to the conditions of the arrangements, they agree that certain basic conditions will be met, as mentioned or deFined in federal legislation, in this case.

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
For about one year, I have been involved in this area, together with other members of this House. I notice that the member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) is here this afternoon. I happen to know that the member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead) will be speaking later on, and other members of the committee have already taken the floor, including the member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), the member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) and the member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I know that the member for Vercheres (Mr. Loiselle) is to speak Monday.
Mr. Speaker, our experience on this committee has been, once again I must use the word unique, because I believe that for the first time, we have succeeded in making this very complex matter of federal-provincial relations understandable to the public. Hearings were held across the country, in all provincial and territorial capitals and in Ottawa, and Canadians came forward to discuss federal-provincial relations as these concerned them directly. I feel this was a healthy process, and I know that it was a very satisfying experience for all members who took part. We have learned a great deal about this great and diverse country of ours.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have carefully read and listened to the debate on this bill and I think it has been an interesting one. It has been informative and I believe that most of the members who spoke on it have a better knowledge of fiscal arrangements and probably the best knowledge and information on this question than they ever had before, when these very complex negotiations took place and we were confronted with a bill in the House of Commons without having had any ventilation of the issue at all.
The way in which Parliament was used, the way Members of Parliament were given the opportunity, adequate staff and resources to study the question and hold hearings has been of help to the government and to Parliament in debating this issue. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The practice should be expanded.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes, it should be expanded. I recognize the sincerity the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) had when he was government House leader for a short period in his attempts to find ways to make these smaller committees work. I am happy the government borrowed that page from the short-lived government of which the hon. member was a part. I hope, as the hon. member suggests, that it will be expanded in future, as I believe it is helpful to the government.
We should not conclude that the government has to accept in detail every recommendation of a committee for it to be a success. That is a falsehood. The government maintains its
decision-making influence. All the government does is delay its decision-making. In the meantime, we can have a better debate because we have more information and perhaps more controversy. Then the government decides.
The public and this House should not judge the value of a parliamentary task force on the basis of how many recommendations the government accepts from its report. The government may have valid reasons for not accepting some recommendations. What the report of a parliamentary committee does is force the government to answer why it does not accept certain recommendations. In that sense, a debate is better and the public is better served.
I want to deal with a matter raised by my friend with whom I spent some very interesting months last summer, the hon. member for Mississauga South. He wondered how the Liberals are going to vote on this bill. In particular, he wanted to know how I was going to vote because, in his view, the proposal of the government is very far from the report of the parliamentary task force.
I disagree with the hon. member that there is a wide gap between the report, the position of the government and the outcome of the negotiations, when you consider the overall aspect not only of the established programs financing, but the elimination of the revenue guarantee and the equalization program. Those are the payments by the federal government to the provincial treasuries.
I recognize that in the case of EPF some tax points were transferred to the provinces in 1977. It was part of a deal at that time. While those tax points are provincial revenues, they must continue to be included when measuring the federal government's contribution. The government is not misleading anyone when it counts them. It is not denying that they are provincial revenues. Nevertheless, they have to be counted as a measure of the federal contribution.
There is another element that should be considered. The budget changes proposed by the government on November 12 will have the effect of increasing the federal tax base by approximately $2.5 billion to $3 billion. This will automatically increase revenues to those provinces which are part of the tax collection agreement and use the federal tax base as their base and a percentage of that base to collect their tax revenues. Quebec has its own tax collection system and must be measured in another way.
In eliminating the revenue guarantee, the government is maintaining the financing of the programs as they were defined before 1977. I will not get into that disagreement now. When you consider the payments from the federal EPF and equalization, they are not far from a value that could be imputed to the recommendations in our report. There is a difference, but they are not that far apart.
In political terms, while the increase in provincial revenues resulting from the increase in the federal tax base is not a federal transfer, it is more income tax moneys which the provincial governments will collect merely because of a
March 26, 1982

political decision of this Parliament. We must take the flak for increasing the federal tax base. It is to the credit or debit of the Parliament of Canada, and the provinces will benefit.
In terms of political morality, it is not so bad as to say that, while we are eliminating the revenue guarantee, we are provoking additional revenues of $685 million to provincial treasuries in the next fiscal year, which begins next week.
In judging the total government response, while I admit it is not to the last number the same value as in our report, it is close enough for me to accept it. What makes me accept it even more is that, apart from the fact the government did follow many of our recommendations, a very important one of which gives a single entitlement, as well as others that the government accepted, the equalization program is being made much more generous than it was by the inclusion of local taxes for municipal services.

Mr. Speaker, it should be pointed out that the fiscal equalization system is going to be far more generous to the Atlantic provinces, because of the computation formula that will be included in the act, and the basis on which payments will be calculated. Now, the representative average will be the average per capita yield of five provinces, namely, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. When the representative average of these provinces is calculated, and since the per capita yield includes municipal taxes and local charges for municipal services, the four Atlantic provinces are going to be much better off, because traditionally, their property taxes, which are raised by the municipalities, have been very low. In Ontario, for instance, and British Columbia, which I know better, and I believe the same applies to Quebec, municipal taxes have always been very high. Because taxes are high in the five provinces and lower in the four Atlantic provinces, it means that in the long run, the equalization program will be far more advantageous for us, because on the whole-I am of course speaking generally-towns in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, in fact any small community, will have lower municipal taxes than the City of Ottawa, for instance. In Ottawa, I believe that property taxes, which include school taxes, for a house worth about $100,000, would be around $1,200 or $1,500 per year.

Or even more, as my colleague for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) just said. In my own province, in New Brunswick, for instance, we would probably pay $500 or $600 in municipal taxes. So that under the equalization system, an average figure is calculated for the five provinces I mentioned earlier, and the federal treasury then pays the province of New Brunswick the difference between, for instance, its own municipal taxes and the average calculated for the five provinces. Clearly, by broadening the base for equalization purposes, the four Atlantic provinces stand to benefit considerably in the long run.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
With respect to how I would vote on the bill, I would vote for it because it is close enough to the task force report that I am satisfied that, first, we have influenced the government during the negotiations, and second, because the report must be seen as a consensus. I read carefully what the member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill said in his interpretation of the report. Again, one should not be too surprised to find that when politicians from different parties and different regions of the country have arrived at a consensus on a document after negotiations which must take place in order to agree to any coherent political statement, they have slightly varying interpretations of what the consensus is. That is what consensus is all about.
The day that you try to have another form of consensus, that system of trying to arrive at a consensus will break down. I do not believe the hon. member was fair when he stated that, in his view, the government ignored the recommendations of the task force. He said that the report rejected the government's claim that there was a fiscal imbalance. I would refer him and the House to page 33 of our report. He is entitled to his opinion and, being a politician, and one from the New Democratic Party, I knew he would put his own interpretation to the consensus, even if he agreed with the report. I have not been fooled because I expected that. However, the explanation of the task force is much broader on the question of fiscal imbalance than the selective words that the member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill decided to quote. Page 33 of the report says:
The federal deficits registered in recent years can, however, be explained partly in terms of discretionary counter-cyclical fiscal policy-a deliberate attempt to maintain employment at a time of world recession. In addition, the various tax expenditure measures introduced since the 1972 implementation of tax reform, as well as the indexation of the personal income tax system, have deprived the federal treasury-as well as provincial treasuries-of substantial amounts of money, and unusually high debt service charges have compounded the difficulty.
That is another interpretation of the consensus of the task force from that which the member had. The report goes on to say:
What is undeniable is that the federal government faces a major budgetary problem in the size of the public debt and corresponding debt service charges.
Members can read further if they wish, but I will move on to page 34 in order to make my point more succinctly. It says:
The federal government is at an interesting intermediate point on the spectrum between these two extremes, a point where a prolonged cyclical budget deficit begins to lead to some aspects of a persistent structural imbalance. The structural problem emerges because the size of the debt accumulated to date begins to constrain to an unacceptable degree the margin of manoeuvre in federal government decisions on fiscal policy.
The hon. member and some in the press have said that we categorically rejected the interpretation of the Minister of Finance of some fiscal imbalance is wrong. In the first place, the minister never said there was a fiscal imbalance. He said there had been a shift in the balance between the amount of money that the federal government was collecting some 20

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
years ago and what it is collecting now in terms of the percentage of the fiscal pie, how much the federal government is spending and how much the provincial and local governments are spending. That is what the Minister of Finance said.
What we did was to study the two different kinds of imbalances, one of which was structural. We tried to determine what "structural" would have meant. That is what we said did not exist. What we meant was that no level of government in Canada has the taxation resources within the Constitution to deliver or discharge its constitutional responsibilities. That does not exist in Canada and the government has never said it did. The Minister of Finance never said it existed. What we have is an imbalance which has occurred over the years because of what I mentioned earlier, the discretionary countercyclical fiscal policy. We mention the tax expenditure measures. The government is taking steps to attempt to close the tax expenditure accounts.
I recognize that the Conservative members on the task force would not agree with these measures for too long, even if these tax expenditures were probably more acceptable to their philosophies than they were to the hon. member from the NDP. But now he says that the government is moving to close some of the "loopholes", as he calls them. The hon. member says that he would have closed other loopholes. That is a matter of political choice, but to suggest that the government did not take steps to deal with its deficit problem by closing the tax expenditure accounts is not true. The hon. member can disagree if he wishes, and I respect him for that. Obviously, whenever the government proposes to close the tax expenditure account in one area, he will say, "You should not touch that one, you should touch the other one". That is the political game. But generally, we came to an agreement and that is the first point that I want to make about the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill.
I was sorry to hear the member for Mississauga South use examples such as spending on CIDA, the budget of the CBC, the budget of the Commissioner of Official Languages, as well as other budgets, to make his point that we could have cut back in those areas and not reduce transfers to the provinces. He is entitled to make his own political judgments as to where cuts can take place. However, there is one point which is undeniable, and it is that over the years, due to cyclical reasons-he said that because he agreed to the statement on page 34-the structural problem emerges because the size of the debt accumulated to date begins to constrain to an unacceptable degree the margin of manoeuvre in federal government decisions on fiscal policy.
This next Fiscal year, approximately 22 per cent of the federal government's budget will be allocated to service the national debt, and over 20 per cent of the budget will be automatically transferred to the provinces. That is a total of 42 per cent which is entirely undiscretionary on the part of the government-that is, unless the government decides to come to Parliament and change the fiscal arrangements, which could not be done when you consider the political reality of this country.
When you take into consideration the other payments that are made directly to individuals, there is not too much money left for Parliament to deal with. I say "Parliament", because let us not give the people the impression that only the Liberals can make decisions on this. The Liberal government of the day can and should be influenced by the opposition as to what should be spent and where. It is often the case that it is influenced.

speechtext: When?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) asks when. Last year he and I were part of another very good political experience when we were on the parliamentary task force on North-South relations. It was as a result of this vigorous efforts in that experience, and partly because of his political support which he obtained from his party, that provoked additional appropriations on the part of the government. Backbenchers on the government side with the help of the opposition pushed the government into changing the trend of a decreasing appropriation to development assistance as a percentage of our GNP, recommended to the government that this trend be changed, and it was. Last year there was a 19 per cent increase in the development assistance budget. This year there is something in the area of 14 per cent or 15 per cent.
Why I say that there is not much room left to manoeuvre, even if opposition members disagree on the appropriations of the government, as they must, is that they should consider that it is the Parliament of Canada which will be strapped and stifled and incapable of carrying out its responsibilities in the international field, in the field of communications such as the CBC, in the fields of official bilingualism, national defence, and energy. So it is not the federal government of the day; it is the Parliament of Canada. What happens the day the Parliament of Canada has no more funds to appropriate when it must appropriate 42 per cent to the service of the debt and to transfers to the provinces? I do not know exactly what the percentage will be in 1982-83 with regard to payments to individuals for old age pensions, family allowances and so forth, but I venture to say it will be about 25 per cent. So there is not that much money left for there to be discretion on the part of the federal government in its spending. That has to be recognized.
I will prove in a minute that the only provinces the elimination of the revenue guarantee will affect to any important degree, if at all, will be the provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. With the improvements to the equalization program, the other provinces will gain. What must be considered here is the increase in total equalization, and the increase in EPF which will continue to be indexed to the gross national expenditure. Over all, with the exception of those four provinces, there will be no effect to any important degree. When we consider the offsets from the increases in the federal tax base, in some cases the transfers will be much more generous.
March 26, 1982

I will provide figures to prove what I am talking about. Let us begin with the province of Newfoundland. The entitlement of the province of Newfoundland in 1981-82 to equalization is $431 million. The entitlement for 1982-83 is $522 million. It will increase from $431 million in 1981-82 to $799 million in 1986-87. EPF cash transfers to Newfoundland will be reduced by $5 million because of the elimination of the revenue guarantee, but the tax transfer will go up by $9 million, and the offsets from increases in provincial revenues, because of the increase in the federal tax base, will be $6 million. So for Newfoundland in 1982-83 the total increase in its revenues because of budget changes and because of fiscal arrangements changes will be from a base of $652 million in 1981-82 to $753 million in 1982-83. That is how generous this program will be. That is a $101 million increase.
Even if hon. members want to disagree politically-and we can have different philosophical perspectives as to how we should deal with the economy in a period of fiscal restraint- all hon. members who are responsible must admit that there has to be some restraint, and if the federal government must restrain its own expenditures on the things it has to do under the Constitution, as it is doing, surely the provincial governments should be able to accept-particularly the four richest ones I mentioned-some degree of adjustment. However, the equalization recipient provinces should not have to, and that is why the program is acceptable to me as a Liberal.
In the case of the four Atlantic provinces, Quebec and Manitoba there will not be reductions when we consider the matter over all. There will be very generous increases. I want to state emphatically to students and administrators in postsecondary education institutions in the four Atlantic provinces-I have looked at the numbers more carefully for those provinces-that there is no justification at all to say there are federal cutbacks because there are no cutbacks in those provinces to squeeze the students and administrators of those institutions. I say this also to health boards and health commissions in Atlantic communities. There is no justification for saying there are federal cutbacks in relation to these services, including hospitals, because in the province of Newfoundland there will be an increase in one year of $101 million. In the province of Prince Edward Island there is a $23 million increase, from $150 million in 1981-82 to $173 million. Someone else can work out the percentages. In Nova Scotia the increase in 1982-83 will be from $863 million to $986 million. That is a $123 million increase when considered over all, and that is how this must be considered.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What about Ontario? Do you have figures for Ontario?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I have Figures for Ontario, but let me put the figures for my province on the record first. With respect to New Brunswick, when we consider the equalization entitlement for this year and next year we see that there will be an increase from $415 million to $490 million. When we consider equalization, EPF cash and tax, even after the elimination of the revenue guarantee, and when we consider the increases in
Federal Transfers to Provinces
provincial revenues because of increases in the federal tax base, we see that the total increases are from $695 million to $786 million. However, we do not even have to consider the provincial revenues because of the federal tax base. Some hon. members say we have no business counting those revenues because they are provincial taxes. Let us say I agree with that. Even without that, for Newfoundland the total in 1981-82 is $652 million. In 1982-83 it is $747 million, and it increases and increases by an average of between 12 per cent and 13 per cent a year for the next five years.
Let us consider my own province. In 1981-82 the total is $695 million, and I do not include in that the increases because of the federal tax base. In 1982-83 it is $778 million. There are increases; the numbers are there. There is no justification at all for the provinces of New Brunswick, Newfoundland, P.E.I. or Nova Scotia-I say this emphatically, and I am ready to defend it anywhere-to allege there are federal cutbacks because of the fact that we are eliminating the revenue guarantee. That was only one little part of the fiscal transfer. When we consider this overall, we find they are all getting very generous increases.
Let me refer to Ontario. The hon. member asked about Ontario. The EPF cash transfer was $2,367 billion in 1981-82. That will be reduced to $2,297 billion in 1982-83 because of the elimination of the revenue guarantee. The EPF tax transfer will go up from $1,703 billion to $1,989 billion. That continues to go up. Let us consider the net revenue increase due to the budget tax changes. That has to be considered because Ontario, without taking any political flak and without changing the tax laws in its provincial House, will collect more provincial income tax, $171 million. The total in Ontario goes up from $4,071 billion-and Ontario is not exactly a poor province-to $4,457 billion.
