subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak on Bill C-97 today, amending the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977. I am sure that most Canadians do not realize the extent to which the federal and provincial governments have had historically, and will have in the future, a fiscal relationship that affects the day to day lives of every one of us as citizens.
Bill C-97 will effect very major changes to that transfer program. In 1981-82, under the equalization program federal tax dollars were transferred to the provinces to the extent of $3.6 billion; hospital insurance, approximately $2.8 billion; medicare, approximately $1 billion; extended health care, $700 million; post-secondary education, $1.8 billion; and Canada Assistance Plan, some $2 billion.
The taxpayers of the nation pay part of their money to the federal government and part of their money to the provincial governments, for which they receive services and the benefit of equalization payments made directly to provincial governments. For example, they receive hospital insurance, medicare, post-secondary education, welfare and social assistance. We should never forget that the taxpayers of Canada pay for these services. This was driven home to me more than anything else when I sat as one of the two Progressive Conservative members on the federal task force which looked into transfers. The last speaker, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), was the chairman of the committee. He did a first-class job.
I should like to talk about the results of the work of the task force. It was a fascinating process. Naturally we in the House
Federal Transfers to Provinces
are in an adversarial system, because Fiberals have a vision as to what they want for the country and we have a vision as to what we would do for the country. Those visions are different with regard to the role of individuals and that of the state. We also know that committees tend to be rather adversarial, but Parliament has come up with the mechanism of a task force. We have had seven task forces. In the case of the one to which I referred, there were four Fiberal members, two Conservatives and a member of the NDP. The members of the task force were all backbenchers. The purpose of the task force was for us to direct our minds to the problem. Rather than from the perspective of politics, we approached the problem with the idea of seeing if we could, from the evidence we gathered, come up with some solutions to recommend to our fellow members of Parliament. This is exactly what we did. Over the course of four months we travelled across the entire country. We talked to people who were actually delivering medicare, such as doctors and nurses. Also we talked to university administrators, students, people administering welfare programs and to members of provincial governments, including members of the cabinets and of the legislatures. A large number of common sense recommendations resulted from the work of the task force. If the government felt obliged to adopt them, I am sure the country would be much stronger.
I should like to make a few comments about the fiscal history of the country. As in the case of everything else, we are not addressing this problem in a vacuum. We have had a long history of federal-provincial relations which started with confederation. Section 91 of the BN A Act gave certain powers to the federal government, and Section 92 gave certain powers to the provincial governments. Prior to the 1930s or prior to the Second World War, some 70 per cent of public government moneys were spent by the provinces and some 30 per cent were spent through Parliament. As a result of the outbreak of World War II, the provinces gave up their taxing powers to the federal government because we wanted to finance the war. In that national effort, provinces gave up their taxing powers over their citizens to the federal government, pursuant to Section 92 of the BNA Act. At that time some 70 per cent of revenues were spent by the federal government and some 30 per cent through the provincial governments. We can see that it was a total reversal of what existed before the Second World War. Since that war there has been a gradual transfer of additional cash and tax points from the federal government back to the provinces, so that by about 1980 it was back to where it was before World War II, that is, some 70 per cent of the money was spent through the provinces and some 30 per cent through Parliament.
When citizens hear the government say that it is losing its fiscal capacity, that it is being weakened and that it must be strengthened, perhaps it is a legitimate political point of view, but if we look at the history of it we are back to where we were before. This is consistent with the country being a federation. We are so broad and diverse, with such differing provincial

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
interests, that most people want their provinces to be significant in their lives. Most people feel that provinces are more responsive to them than we are in the House of Commons. This is understandable. When we superimpose Canada upon Europe, we realize that it goes from the west coast of Ireland, across Ireland, across England, across the Netherlands and Germany, through Poland and beyond the Ural Mountains in Russia. If we look at the various countries in Europe that operate in areas much smaller than that of Canada and compare them with what we have done in Canada with one federal government and ten provincial governments, I think we should be incredibly proud.
We shall always have federal-provincial conflicts, but the government should not say that the nation will fall because the sharing of tax and public revenue has now returned to what it was before the Second World War, no more than it did during the war when 70 per cent of the money was collected in Ottawa in the national interest.
We require fiscal flexibility so that during times of national crises or war financial power and decision making can flow to the centre and we can act as a nation. During peacetime there will be a natural filtering out and flowing of taxing authority and spending power to the provinces as a reflection of our huge country and its very diverse regions. As the task force travelled across the country, I did not find any objection to a mechanism which would be flexible enough so power and cash could flow to the federal government in an emergency. As I said, during the war the federal government took the taxing power from the provinces by way of a tax rental agreement. Since that time we have entered into a period of five-year agreements which are commonly called "tax collection agreements". The last one was negotitated in 1976-77. In the past, negotitions at each of those five-year periods were carried out between governments. Then a bill was presented in the House and in the provincial legislatures. This was felt by some of us in Parliament to be entirely not satisfactory from the perspective of representing our constituents. Therefore, the government agreed to the opposition request to set up this task force to travel across the country and come up with a large number of recommendations.
The process is correct now; Members of Parliament should have input. I hope the government agrees to this in the future. The real question is whether, compared with the 1977 agreement, the government would be cutting back the amount of cash it would transfer to the provinces, if it were extended for the next five-year period? The answer in terms of cash is absolutely undisputed-there is a cutback in cash transfers to the provinces. The amount of that cash cutback is what the federal government now refers to as the revenue guarantee.
I want to show that the government is cutting back, and that it should not be hiding it by trying to say that it is doing away with something which existed in 1971. The government should come out and say that it is cutting back money because of the deficit, because the provinces have been unreasonable, because it wants to decide how to spend more cash, or any number of other reasons. Why should the government not be honest and
straightforward? It should not come up with the fraudulent excuse of the revenue guarantee. The fact of the matter is that in 1971, there was a new tax regime which was brought in by Edgar Benson. As the five-year agreement was negotiated, there was a great deal of uncertainty as to whether the provinces, under the new taxing mechanism, would have the same cash flow. Therefore, the federal government said that it would give them a guarantee, and that took place. Then in 1976 the parties got together again to negotiate the new five-year contract from 1977 to 1982. Both the federal and the provincial governments had a position. Under the 1971 agreement there was a cost-sharing agreement, dollar for dollar, but the actual costs of operating health care and post-secondary education were going up enormously. Both levels of government agreed there had to be a cutback. They agreed there would be a base amount of funding by the federal government and between 1977 and 1982 that base would go up by a delayed three-year average of the gross national product. That was part of the negotiated settlement.
The question of the revenue guarantee was discussed. Health care and post-secondary education agreements were not coming up until 1980. Because the federal government would have been forced to continue paying dollar for dollar, it offered $7.60 per capita plus one tax point provided the provinces would give up extending those two agreements to 1980. That was the negotiated settlement. It is like you and I meeting and each of us making an offer and negotiating back and forth. We would then come to an agreement. That was it. The federal govenment then put in a base amount to be escalated by the three-year delayed average of the GNP.
The revenue guarantee effectively died. It no longer was a part of the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements agreement. That is why I say that it is really perverse for the federal government in 1982 to refer back to 1971 and forget entirely about the agreement of 1976. I would rather see the government be straight and honest and say "We are going to cut back the money, folks, because of one, two, three and four reasons." Let us not hear any of these silly reasons because that causes a breakdown in trust and relationships between levels of government and here in the House. I do not want to be part of any sort of fraudulent deal. Why do we not just face the situation? If we feel that Parliament needs to have more money here and less money for the provinces, let us face that directly.
Proof of that lies in a speech made by Donald Macdonald, as reported in Hansard, when he said that it was a deal and we gave them $7.60 and a tax point, and that ended the revenue guarantee.
I want to speak about equalization for a minute. There is no doubt that it is a program which is found in virtually every federation. But here in Canada we have come up with our own method. We have bounced around from national averages to a two-province proposal. The last agreement was back to a national average. Now we are basing our calculations on the
March 26, 1982

average GNP of some of the more wealthy provinces, excluding the Atlantic provinces. I do not see any problem with that. A five province average GNP is a good standard upon which to base equalization payments. I did not agree with the original suggestion that they should be based upon the average GNP in Ontario alone, because Ontario is in the process again, as a result of federal government unilateral actions, of effectively de-industrializing. Let me tell you why that is so.
Some ten years ago, the federal government decided that if the price of energy went up Canadians were going to be insulated from that. In other words, we were not going to be blackmailed by any of the Arab states. Therefore, the federal government made a unilateral decision to keep down the price of oil. But that sent out signals to the car manufacturers to continue producing big cars. It sent signals to Canadians to continue buying them. That is exactly what we did. But meanwhile Japan and Germany had no choice but to go to world price for oil. The top brains and engineers in Japan and Germany immediately directed their minds toward producing more efficient cars and engines. As a result, now, ten years later, we cannot compete with them. They beat us at every turn. Most Canadians losing jobs in the Windsor corridor do not realize that it was as a result of a government decision ten years ago to somehow deny reality. That is what happens when governments get involved. It does not matter of which political stripe they are. It is the function of a government that is too big and tries to protect people, for political purposes, which it is unable to do.
If you give a 10 per cent subsidy to an industry, Mr. Speaker, I can guarantee you that within two or three years that industry will be 10 per cent inefficient. Meanwhile, other countries that do not have the benefit of subsidies face reality. They produce within reality and they can beat the country with a subsidized industry.
Equalization is a good program. It is uniquely Canadian and it is now entrenched in our Constitution. Each area in turn over the course of Canadian history has been wealthy. Before confederation, for a while, the Atlantic provinces were wealthy compared to Ontario and Quebec. After confederation, Ontario became a wealthy province and contributed net benefits. We in the west were recipients. In the east they were contributors. Now we in the west are net contributors to the national good. That is the way it should be. We are proud to make those contributions. It may be that in 25 years from now the fish off the Atlantic coast, the oil in Hibernia or the oil in the north will bring more money into the central coffers. We may once again in Alberta be a have-not province. We can all operate with the east being strong for a few decades and then the west. Perhaps the pendulum will swing again depending upon the ebb and flow of world affairs and whatever is "hot" at the time. Clearly, we want to protect that equalization policy.
The other major program, commonly defined as the established programs financing, covers health insurance, medicare and post-secondary education. As I say, there is no doubt that these programs are being cut because of the revenue guarantee. There will be less cash transferred to the provinces. That is
Federal Transfers to Provinces
a situation we should be facing head on. The real problem comes again because provinces are like people; some have more wealth than others. Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan will not be hurt that much by the cutbacks because they are wealthy provinces at this time. But the seven provinces east of Saskatchewan all have substantial deficits. To take a cut in cash transfers will have a great impact on them.
The real questions are, first, what is the fiscal capacity of government and second, which level of government has the strongest fiscal capacity to handle the deficit? Obviously the answer is the federal government. The federal government can tax all the people of this country. It can tax all of the northern lands and the oil and gas flowing from there. It can tax the oil and gas flowing offshore, both on the east and on the west coasts. But compare that kind of taxation with what can happen in Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Island has 125,000 people and a few more potatoes than that. Its tax base is restricted basically to an agricultural type of economy, whereas Alberta can tax the oil production industry, the oil service industry, the oil refining industry and a very rich agricultural industry because of irrigation.
The federal government can tax by any means and mode. The real question Canadians should ask is which level of government can best handle the deficit. Clearly, it has to be the federal government. For the Liberal government now to transfer some of its deficit to the backs of the seven provinces east of Saskatchewan strikes me as being wrong. I would rather see the government face this problem directly. If Canadians need to have a tax increase to counter that, so be it. For years and years the federal Liberal government has been offering all sorts of attractive programs to Canadians, preserving for them that low capitalistic tax. The difference was made up by borrowing under the table. You can get away with that for a while. The national debt was $5 billion, then $10 billion and then $20 billion. But now the national debt is something like $100 billion. The interest alone to service that debt costs $17 billion. Some 20 per cent plus of every tax dollar just services the debt. So now we see the government having to apply socialist taxes to meet socialist programs.

Now we are getting the taxes to match the program, and business is dropping away. I certainly believe, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a higher level of debate in the House over the last few days as a result of this fiscal task force which the hon. member for Gloucester chaired. He did a first-class job and, if I may say so, I think the rest of us did also, including the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead). We found that

Federal Transfers to Provinces
Canadians have no problem in wearing both a federal and a provincial hat. They recognize that their money goes to both the federal and provincial governments. The overriding recommendation and advice they gave to us was: "Listen, you crazy politicians, make the system work. You have a duty to make the system work". They told us that again and again. Then we came back to our colleagues in the House and told them that Canadians want it to work. Co-operative federalism is the reality of this nation, and as elected representatives we have an obligation to make it work. We also found that the task force process was a good one, and we hope our colleagues will buy it in the future when the next agreement comes up, I suppose in 1987.
In dealing with the established programs financing we found it necessary to separate the programs, so we recommended that health insurance be separate from other programs and that it receive 67.9 per cent of the 1981-82 contributions. Postsecondary education, which we found to be a very unique area, should receive 32.1 per cent. It is unique simply because of our unique confederation. In 1867, because of its critical importance to the people of Quebec with regard to language and culture, education was left to the provinces under Section 92 of the BNA Act. Consequently, technically the federal government should have no say in it. But during the 1950s and 1960s when education became an important priority to Canadians, the federal government became involved because it had this massive taxing and spending power I mentioned earlier. This resulted in money being transferred to the provinces.
In spite of the fact the federal government puts a lot of money into education, we found, because of the Constitution and because of the very deep feelings of the people of Quebec, which go beyond all provincial parties, that the federal government basically had to be restricted to being not much more than a source of money. However, there is no doubt that the provinces over the past five years have not honoured their 1976 commitment to let the federal government share in the decision making, at least with respect to identifying national goals.
I have no hesitation in speaking against the provincial Conservative governments. They were too protective of their jurisdiction and should not now be seen to be whining and snivelling when the federal government says, "We wants to have more say in the matter, and either you give us a role or we will cut back". The provinces were too aggressive. Had they shared a little more, they could have helped the situation and we probably would not be in this position today. I have no hesitation in directing that toward all provincial governments, sir.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government has to get its own house in order with respect to education. We recommended the creation of a focal point so that federal government contributions can be co-ordinated and synchronized. I did not hear the hon. member for Gloucester refer to that and I am not sure whether the government has accepted the recommendation in our task force study for the appointment of a central co-ordinator for federal programs. I hope the
hon. member will follow that up because I do believe it to be a sound recommendation.
Then there were recommendations dealing with students. As a result of federal cutbacks even in the revenue guarantee portion there is no doubt some provinces will have to increase tuition fees. That will have a serious effect because the one thing we achieved during the 1950s, starting with John Diefen-baker and carrying through the Pearson era, was that thousands of children from modest income families were able, through low tuition and the accessibility of universities, to go to university. Having done so, they were then able to go out in the world and build fascinating careers for themselves. Now, to the extent the revenue guarantee is cut back, the provinces, particularly those east of Saskatchewan, will have to increase tuition fees. There is no doubt that this will affect accessibility, which in turn will affect the capacity of this nation to build its future and become the most powerful and popular nation in the entire world.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, when the government cuts back on the revenue guarantee it should at least couple that with a solid commitment of funds to the Canadian student loan program so that those who wish to take on that burden will have it interest free until they are working and making a living. Most students would be prepared to take on that burden if they could have some help during the early years, such as this interest-free provision. We could also have a creative combination of grants and loans perhaps to cover the first year of university. Students would decide whether or not they like university, and if they do then they could have an additional loan and a smaller grant for the second year. The same would apply to the third and fourth years and on into graduate school. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, that is not to be because the government has not announced an increase of funding to the loan program, and I very much fear that many students in the eastern provinces will lose the opportunity of attending university. To that extent the cutbacks are truly a tragedy in their lives.

That program has some very real problems attaching to it because it relates to a matter that affects us all dramatically, particularly as we come into our old age and start to lose our health. We want to have access not only to doctors but to good hospitals, to medical treatment, to drugs; it deals with doctors' incomes, and with extra billing and with service to people and to user fees.
We should recognize at the start that we are attempting to balance the very legitimate interests of the users, the doctors, the hospital support staffs and of the taxpayers of the country. There is no doubt as to the reality of the fact that the incomes of general practitioners are down. I think that is not so with respect to specialists, but it certainly is so with respect to family care doctors. To the extent that we injure our doctors and we affect their status and their belief in themselves, we are going to be hurting ourselves as citizens.
We all know the history, that prior to medicare doctors were self-employed individuals, they set up their own offices, they provided their own staff, they provided for their own pensions, out of the fee for service. A person went to a doctor and paid a fee. That fee was variable, depending on what the doctor felt. Oftentimes it was nothing, sometimes it was a great deal, depending upon the wealth of the recipient. It was a fee for service. Doctors had a real status in our community, and for that status and the ability to be self-employed they were prepared to hire the staff, to provide their own pensions and to work very, very hard. I do not think there is a person in this building who would deny the reality of the contribution that doctors made in those early days, with their horse and buggy and in their cars, going out at all hours of the night. That is a
Federal Transfers to Provinces
tribute which certainly is deserved in the community where I come from being a farm boy from the prairies.
They also had at that time a very special relationship which they described as the doctor-patient relationship. Then we got medicare, and again there was a feeling across the country that not everybody had access to doctors, that somehow it was demeaning for some to take medical services and not to be paid. Therefore, again the government became involved and it said: "We will step in, folks, we will guarantee you service" and they imposed a system upon the provinces. So the new factor was no longer a patient-doctor relationship, in terms of a health relationship or a fee relationship; there was now a doctor, a patient and a third party, government, and the government was setting the fee schedule. As a result, over a period of time, the charts show clearly that the incomes of general practitioners have dropped vis-a-vis other status people in the community.
Personally I feel we are in the process of destroying our health care. I feel badly about it because I think it is a product of government with its bureaucracy and its indirect lack of understanding by politicians of the true relationship and what happens out in the field.
Mr. Speaker, you will note that the task force recommended that extra billings be banned. I stand with the doctors 100 per cent in their opposition to the banning of extra billing, because that will genuinely fix in place a dishonest system. We should be, more than anything else, honest. If Canadians want to Have their doctors as civil servants, let us turn to the doctors, let us say: "Look, that is what they want; therefore wp will pay you a salary equal to that of Members of Parliament, that is $65,000." Really, I suppose we would have to pay them $75,000 because we get $16,600 tax free. Let us offer the doctors $75,000 as a salary, let us provide their staff for them, as the people do for us and as we do for staff doctors and for lawyers who work for us. Let us provide them with their offices, let us provide them with a pension plan as generous as ours. If that were done, you would have virtually 100 per cent of the doctors under the plan. Now they have the worst of all worlds. They have the so-called image of being self-employed and all the decoction of it, but they are not because their fees are set, and yet they are expected to provide their offices and their staff. So why do we not offer to take over all of their offices? It would cost the Canadian people several billions of dollars, but at least it would be honest and the doctors would be working 37 hours a week.
Some people say there are too many doctors in this country. The only reason there are too many doctors is that they are all working 60 and 70 hours a week. If the doctors were working the hours that our civil service work or the hours that are worked in most industries, 37 hours a week, there would not be too many doctors. If they can make $75,000 a year, have their pension provided for as we do, we would have no trouble.
So my plea to you, as fellow members, is this. We should face it directly. Either we want doctors as civil servants and we will make the necessary adjustment, or we are prepared to

leave them as self-employed, independent people. We have to give them more freedom on their billing or we have to set up a mechanism where by they would truly know that they have power to get what they feel they deserve.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians must decide, because there is no doubt that the medicare system is failing. We have examples from other countries. Britain adopted a system which has tried to create the illusion of self-dependent doctors but with the government setting the fees. As a result, the system has deteriorated to the point where patients are assigned now to a doctor. In Britain you do not have the freedom to go to the doctor you choose, particularly if you are poor. You are directed to doctor A, and if you do not like him that is tough luck for you, you have a terribly difficult time shifting. At the same time, the doctor has his patient load assigned to him, and as a result there is opting out.
If there is anyone who thinks doctors can be prevented from opting out, they will find it cannot be done, because they will operate in their own homes if they want to. Then you get a two-tier system.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to begin speaking this afternoon on Bill C-97. I am pleased to follow my two colleagues on the task force, the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), and the chairman of the task force, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). It was a seven-man all-party parliamentary committee. As the previous speaker said, we worked very hard and intensively from March to July of last year, and finally published the report in August. The report, which has been mentioned in the House on different occasions, is the first
March 26, 1982

report of its kind dealing with fiscal federalism in Canada. It will be very useful in the days and years ahead.
In the second part of my remarks, which I will perhaps complete on Monday, I would like to speak more about the task force experience and something of the recommendations of the task force, particularly in the health care and postsecondary education fields.
The government has proposed that national standards for health care be clarified and that an effective mechanism for their maintenance be developed, in consultation with the provinces, for incorporation in new federal legislation by March of next year. The government has also proposed that there should be two full years, until March, 1984, for consultations and discussions of ways of implementing the national objectives with respect to post-secondary education.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his speech to the House on March 22 of this week at page 15681 of Hansard stated that the parliamentary task force had a good deal to say about the program aspects of EPF and that it made some rather helpful proposals in support of the directions in which the government is now moving. I therefore will get back to discussing some of these proposals in a few minutes. However, first it might be useful to summarize some of the main aspects of Bill C-97.
The bill when passed will transfer $105 billion to the provinces in cash and tax points over the next five years under the two major programs of fiscal equalization and established programs financing. Over the past five years $61 billion was contributed to these two programs, and we will be spending on these programs some $44 billion more during the next five years than we have in the past five years. The bill will also provide a new equalization formula.
It is not generally realized that the provinces now spend the largest share of public moneys raised in Canada. Between 1961 and 1981 the federal share of total government revenues declined from 57 per cent to 49 per cent and the provincial and municipal share increased from 43 per cent to 51 per cent. If you deduct federal transfers to provinces from federal revenues and consider them as provincial revenues, the federal share of the total revenue pie has decreased since 1961 from 50 per cent to only 38 per cent today. These numbers indicate that Canada is one of the most fiscally decentralized countries in the western world.
The fiscal equalization program is a cornerstone of the Canadian federation. It seeks to make possible for all provinces to provide reasonable standards of basic public services to their residents without having to resort to unduly high levels of taxation. About $29.3 billion of equalization will be paid to the four Atlantic provinces, Quebec and Manitoba during the next five years, compared to $16.5 billion paid to them during the last five years under the equalization program.
The equalization program has two fundamental components. The first is the measure of provincial fiscal capacity. That is the capacity or potential of a province to raise revenues through taxes of various kinds relative to the capacity of other
Federal Transfers to Provinces
provinces. The bill proposes to broaden the measure of fiscal capacity to include, among other items, municipal taxes and the sale of goods and services by local government. The second basic element is the equalization standard.
Originally the government had proposed to shift to the Ontario standard so that those provinces which did not have the capacity or potential to raise revenues equal to the capacity of Ontario would continue to receive equalization payments.
However, because many of the other provinces were concerned about the economic future of Ontario, the Government of Canada in this bill now proposes a more broadly based standard which will take into account the average taxation capacity of Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
The bill contains a transitional arrangement protecting provinces against too abrupt changes in the level of their equalization and it also contains a ceiling provision under which the growth of total equalization payments to all provinces will not exceed the rate of growth of the Canadian gross national product.
Equalization payments to the six have-not provinces will increase by 13.6 per cent in 1982-83 and by 11.2 per cent on average over the next five years. The transfers made under the Established Programs Financing Act have, since 1977, funded provincial health care and post-secondary education programs. They have also compensated provinces for termination of the 1972 tax reform revenue guarantee.
Under the present system of transferring cash and tax points, the wealthier provinces like Alberta and British Columbia obtained more benefit from their tax points than did the poorer provinces. As recommended by our parliamentary task force, this bill modifies the cash transfers so that the per capita value of total federal contribution to all provinces will be equal. The bill will also end the EPF transfer that compensated the provinces for the 1972 tax reform revenue guarantee. This equalled one personal income tax point and the cash equivalent of a second tax point.
The provinces have argued and are arguing that by ending the revenue guarantee moneys the Canadian government is undermining our support for post-secondary education and health. However, this is definitely not the case. When the premiers met last summer they explicitly declined to include the revenue guarantee as a portion of the federal contribution toward health care and post-secondary education. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall in his 1980 report on health programs also stated that the federal contribution to health programs does not include the two tax points attributable to the revenue guarantee. The government of Canada contribution to these two vital programs will continue to grow over the next five years in line with the increase in the gross national product. The tax measures announced in the November 12 budget for 1982-83 alone will increase provincial revenues by another $685 million.

March 26, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
I wish to re-emphasize that the government's contribution to health care and post-secondary education will increase on an average of 11 per cent per year over the next five years, and so it is ridiculous to say that federal contributions are being cut back. The revenue guarantee program was designed to protect provinces against unforeseen reductions in their revenues which might have resulted from the 1972 tax reforms. It was supposed to end in 1977 but was extended for a further five years. The provinces have had ten years to adjust their taxes to the 1972 tax reforms, and there is no longer any justification to continue the revenue guarantee. In any event, the revenue guarantee in question may make up about 5 per cent of the total amount of moneys that are otherwise being paid to the provinces.
The bill contains certain other items, including allowing the government to transfer to oil producing provinces their share of the federal oil export charge for oil exported from November, 1980, to January, 1982, and to compensate certain provinces with respect to changes in population brought out in the 1981 census.
This bill will enable the federal government to contribute $105 billion for equalization, health care and post-secondary education over the next five years, which emphasizes the strong role that the Government of Canada will continue to play in providing Canadians with the services they need and deserve.
The task force was established last spring as a result of a proposal by the opposition parties which was readily accepted by the government. It included four Liberals: the chairman, the hon. member for Gloucester and hon. members for Vau-dreuil (Mr. Herbert), Vercheres (Mr. Loiselle) and myself; two Conservatives, the vice chairman, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker); and one NDP, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). The task force was empowered to retain the services of a professional staff, and Peter Dobell of the Parliamentary Centre for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade was able to recruit a group of able, knowledgeable and hard-working advisers under Dr. Rodney Dobell of the University of Victoria.
The research branch of the Library of Parliament also provided helpful support, and the research staffs of the three political parties also contributed greatly. The task force produced a set of guidelines and principles-a framework- within which we believe representatives of federal and provincial governments can best negotiate, whatever changes appear appropriate in light of the social goals of these programs and the economic circumstances that prevail as negotiations proceed over the next year or two. The thread that runs through the task force report is not budgetary calculations but accountability in Parliament for federal spending. We concentrated not on the government's expenditure plan but on the institutional changes designed to ensure that Parliament itself can deal more effectively with and be held more fully accountable for federal revenues going directly to provincial governments. We were willing to endorse this report collectively, not
because we all compromised to the point of reaching total consensus on the document, not because we erased all the philosophical differences that separate our positions, but because the report makes clear what some of the differences are. We sincerely believed that what was most important for us as a task force and what is important for us as a country was to work together to arrive at action that was mutually acceptable in light of our different values; not to separate and go our own ways because we cannot agree.
As mentioned, on page six of our report, as we crossed the country, one message was clear-Canadian citizens are more sensitive to what unites them than to what separates them. They are more concerned with a workable federal system than with fine points of jurisdiction. Despite the strains and controversy associated with energy policy, the Constitution, RCMP costs and other inter-governmental frictions, we found that individual Canadians still seem to have little difficulty wearing two hats; as federal taxpayers and voters and as provincial taxpayers and voters. We are heartened to be able to confirm that Canadians remain willing to share their good fortune through interprovincial redistribution and through interregional transfers. They look to the federal government to assure appropriate national standards of access and equity in the programs through which equality of opportunity can be achieved for all Canadians. We encountered few who quarrelled with the need for strong federal leadership in setting out these national standards. Particularly encouraging was the view of many provincial officials and ministers that in cooperative negotiations with their federal counterparts, there would emerge few serious differences on basic national objectives. In short, Canadians are more united than their governments sometimes seem to be-the links that bind them are in reality much stronger than the relations between their governments might suggest.
We held hearings in Ottawa, including evidence from the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the then Secretary of State, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox). We then travelled to the capitals of each of the 12 provinces and territories and met with each of the provincial treasurers or finance ministers, as well as with representatives of the various interest groups, and members of the public at large who are involved with and concerned for our health care system, our post-secondary education system, the funding of our welfare and social services, and our equalization program for the have-not provinces. In addition, we heard views of academic experts, six former premiers of provinces, the Economic Council of Canada, our native peoples and many others.
The members of our task force are very conscious that this was the first occasion on which public consultation and active parliamentary involvement had been possible with respect to reviewing fiscal federalism in Canada, and we therefore recommended that prior to future intergovernmental negotiations on fiscal arrangements, members of Parliament again have a similar opportunity for consultation with the public.
March 26, 1982

Mr. Speaker, I have some more remarks which might be held over to Monday with respect to some of the recommendations regarding health care and post-secondary education. I wonder if I might call it four o'clock?

subsubtopic: EXPENSES INCURRED BY TAXPAYERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of the Department of National Revenue assuming responsibility for the expenses incurred by a taxpayer whom the Department causes to be investigated, when such investigation by the Department's officials does not result in a suit or claim.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have been very anxious to see this motion tabled in the House of Commons and I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this subject. The purpose of the motion is to correct a situation in which many Canadians find themselves. Most members of this House know of similar cases in their ridings. The scenario is always the same. Your secretary puts through an urgent call from one of your constituents, usually a contractor, a businessman or perhaps a pensioner. Then, at the other end a voice says, panic-stricken: They are here. In a flash, you understand that your constituent has just had a visit from the Revenue Canada taxation officers. 1 am not blaming all the department's officers. After all, it is not much fun collecting taxes and income tax. On the other hand, there has been a certain amount of abuse, and I feel that Parliament should be informed.
I shall briefly summarize, if I may, the role of Revenue Canada, Taxation. As all Canadians probably know, personal income tax was introduced in Canada in 1917. When the legislation was passed, Canadians were given the assurance that it was only a temporary measure that would be abolished as soon as the First World War ended. The rest is history, Mr. Speaker. There is a vast store of witty remarks made by taxpayers regarding this temporary measure, which is not expected to disappear very soon. Perhaps this is one example where a government program has been too successful. A
Income Tax
Revenue Canada publication called "Inside Taxation", 1981 edition, tells us that the department took more than $50 billion out of our pockets in 1980-81. That is plenty of money and it explains why we are not about to witness the extinction of our income tax system. The Department of National Revenue is such a profitable business, Mr. Speaker! You can learn a lot by reading the publication "Inside Taxation". You learn that the first function of the Department of National Revenue, Taxation, is the collecting of taxes and other fiscal contributions while deterring fraud and tax evasion. Its second function is maintaining public confidence in the integrity of the taxation system by administering tax legislation fairly, uniformly and courteously. I am emphasizing the word "courteously".
Let me say a few words about courtesy. Of course, for most taxpayers, the payroll deduction system, also called fiscal anesthesia, avoids the need for direct contact with the tax collector. Once a year, every Canadian taxpayer completes a return in which he admits having obtained a certain income and enters as having been deducted from his paychecks, an amount of money which he never had in his pocket, and often is entitled to a small refund. On the other hand, self-employed workers and employers may have closer contacts with the officials of Revenue Canada, Taxation.
Finally, there are taxpayers whose returns are audited and who are provided with revised assessments. How many are there? According to departmental sources, 91,367 returns were checked in 1980-81, which resulted in 70,057 new assessments, and it is with this specific group of Canadian taxpayers that I am concerned. What is the pattern that fits this taxpayer? This constituent who gets in touch with us after having been visited by a taxation officer is often a contractor, a businessman or even a retired person. He has developed a business or a company and employs three, four, five people, often between 20 and 40 people and sometimes more. He pays all his income and other taxes. Most often, he has hired a professional, namely an accountant, to do his bookkeeping, to complete his various tax returns and to provide all the required forms to Revenue Canada, Taxation. One day, he is audited and can then see for himself how the Department of National Revenue goes about enforcing the Canadian tax legislation courteously.
It is unfortunate, but in the cases referred to me, I have found that the Department of National Revenue treats these Canadian citizens literally as though they were criminals. A taxpayer will find that if he is prosecuted by Revenue Canada, Taxation, the burden of proof does not rest on the plaintiff, namely the Department of Revenue, but on the taxpayer himself. It is therefore up to him to prove that he is innocent, hence that Revenue Canada, Taxation is wrong. In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it is easy to see that the department has all the advantage while the taxpayer must spend a lot of money

March 26, 1982
Income Tax
to prove his innocence. When he succeeds, he is simply told: "Sorry, we made a mistake."
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to your attention an article published in Saturday Night magazine in April, 1981. The author quotes Mr. Alan Zener, a lawyer who worked with the Department of Justice and represented Revenue Canada in court. Mr. Zener said, and I quote:
Very often Revenue Canada comes before the courts with very little evidence, but they win their case because the accused, the taxpayer, cannot prove that the assessment notice was incorrect.
This should fly in the face of our sense of justice. However, there is something more serious. Despite the rules that hamper the taxpayers, some of them manage to prove that the assessment notice is incorrect. They win their case. But in order to do so, they have had to spend thousands of dollars in professional fees for lawyers, accountants or tax experts. And this they have to pay. It is in order that this injustice be redressed that I put forward my motion, and I take pleasure in reading it once more, Mr. Speaker, because I find it important:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of the Department of National Revenue assuming responsibility for the expenses incurred by a taxpayer whom the department causes to be investigated, when such investigation by the department's officials does not result in a suit or claim.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the audit branch at Revenue Canada, in addition to not having the burden of proof, has free access to an army of experts within the departments of Finance, Justice and National Revenue. The taxpayer is all by himself, and to get any help he must pay the price. If he happens to win his case, all he is entitled to is a few words of excuse. I am shocked by this. Where the taxpayer can establish that his position was clear and had to incur costs to do so, the Department of National Revenue should compensate for his costs. This in my view might reduce the number of charges against taxpayers, and perhaps even lead Revenue Canada to play a much more significant social role in other terms to humanize Taxation Canada.
The error made by the taxpayers who are investigated by the department of National Revenue is that they do not realize that the litigation, or rather the lawsuit, starts the moment the auditor knocks at his door. The auditor has the right to check everywhere, to require the production of all kinds of documents. This is where the taxpayer needs professional help. Why? The answer is quite simple: If the department goes before the courts, the answers given to the auditor in the course of an investigation may be held as evidence against the taxpayer. So, from the very start, he needs professional help. Sometimes after an investigation the department will close a file and matters will not go before the courts because they would lose their case. However, the taxpayer has proved his innocence at the investigation stage, if I may say so, and to do that he has had to incur costs. My motion is aimed at creating
a mechanism which the Department of National Revenue would use to reimburse the taxpayer's costs.
Mr. Speaker, several methods used by the investigators are unacceptable and border on indecency.
It often happens following some well-defined and specified transactions included in a contract that at the minister's discretion, such a transaction is denounced or cancelled, the burden of the proof always resting with the taxpayer but in most cases nothing is changed. Several tricks are also used and I will take the liberty of mentioning a few. I know many taxpayers who, following the sale of a building or some assets, finally set a price but once again after a visit, the tax assessors, whose specific task is to reassess those transactions, often maintain that the assessment is inflated or excessive.

I have other examples to make my point, Mr. Speaker. I know company owners who have 15, 20 or 30 employees with a weekly payroll between $19,000 and $20,000 and, as everyone knows, they have to send advance payments to the Department of National Revenue on the thirtieth of each month. They have until the fifteenth of the following month to send in that money. Well, believe it or not, some people mail their advance payments on the thirteenth, the fourteenth or the fifteenth of the month. Some officials are

Mr. Speaker,
I wish to speak in support of this motion that the government should consider the advisability of the Department of National Revenue assuming responsibility for the expenses incurred by a taxpayer whom the department causes to be investigated, when such investigation by the department's officials does not result in a suit or claim.
I think this should be extended to cover all federal government departments, as was done in the United States. The problem that the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) will probably run into this afternoon is that one of his Liberal colleagues will talk this excellent motion out. It is one which certainly should be passed because it has much merit.
There is legislation in effect in the United States which covers all federal government departments. A United States senator by the name of Dennis DeConcini introduced a bill which was passed in 1980. After much legislative manoeuvring, the Senate and the House of Representatives passed a final version of Senator DeConcini's equal access to justice act. It was a bill to make federal government more accountable in the enforcement of its regulations. Basically, the bill which became Title II of H. R. 5612, the minority small business contracting bill, will force a government agency to pay legal costs incurred by individuals and small businesses, either in federal court or in an agency-level proceeding, if the agency loses the case and cannot substantially justify its action.
Individuals with a net worth of less than $1 million, businesses with a net worth of less than $5 million and less than 500 employees, and all non-profit organizations and agricultural co-operatives are covered under the legislation. Senator DeConcini claimed that the message was quite simple. He said:
Justice has simply become too expensive for the average American and small businesses, particularly when they are faced with a legal battle against the practically unlimited resources and expertise of the federal government. Many citizens have no recourse; because of the legal costs, they simply knuckle under to the government's demands whether they seem to be justified or not.
This bill not only will make the government more accountable for its actions, it will also provide Congress with a means of finding out how responsible the agencies are being in enforcing their regulations.
In another report of Dennis DeConcini respecting his equal access to justice act, he pointed out:
The law covers only individuals with a net worth of $1 million or less, businesses with a net worth of $5 million or less, and all non-profit organizations and agricultural co-operatives.
It is not, as some opponents have argued, "a threat to the very foundations of the American legal system".
I do not think it would be any threat to the Canadian legal system. He went on to point out:
Lawyers will point out, somewhat accurately, that the principles of equal access run counter to the general legal doctrine that requires each party in a court case to pay his own way. However, that doctrine was formed when the

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on the motion before us. I have had some experience, as have my constituents, dealing with some officers from the Department of National Revenue. It has not always been very pleasant, so I thank the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) for bringing this matter forward.
The first time I had a problem brought to my attention as a member of Parliament, it related to the problems of reassessing. It did not concern reassessment of businesses. In this case it concerned reassessments of people who had hobby farms. These people lived on farms. They wanted to get out of the stinking city for the same reasons as I did, ultimately. They wanted to raise their children in rural settings for all the so-called benefits. They wanted a little more room in which to operate. They wanted to have animals and all that goes with semi-rural life. Since they had small farms, they were encouraged by the government in the form of exemptions and income tax breaks accorded to them. They set up small enterprises on their farms. They were involved in raising bees, cattle, chickens or whatever. In the early years they were able to write off part of their costs, such as those for fencing, development, buildings, telephones and sometimes even special licences for their trucks. However their main income was not from farming, and probably never would be, because their small farms did not have the capacity, certainly in the Fraser Valley, to produce sizeable incomes unless they were accompanied by marketing quotas. Most of these people operated under marketing quotas which allowed them to produce a certain number of eggs, turkeys, milk or whatever.
However, a pattern was established in certain parts of the country wherein such people began receiving visits from very amiable people. These visitors would knock on their doors. They were always very nice, friendly and outgoing. They would introduce themselves, sit down and ask a few questions. Nothing very important would occur and no one would become upset about the visits because they were fine people. Usually the visitors were offered tea, cookies and such. After asking a
few rather penetrating questions, they would depart. A few weeks later the people who had had such visits would receive a nice-looking official envelope from the Department of National Revenue. Lo and behold, they were reassessments. Sometimes the reassessments went back as far as three to five years.

speechtext: Unless there was fraud, no further than four years.

I think the law allowed them to go back five years at that time. Certainly I would be guided by the advice of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) since he is steeped and learned in the law. Nevertheless, sizeable reassessment demands were placed upon these people.
Perhaps someone could say that I am not necessarily speaking to the business of paying for an investigation or for the legal defence thereof when a re-assessment is lost. I am not speaking to that directly, but I am talking about the manner in which these inspectors operated. I am not only referring to the inspectors in this branch of government but in other branches as well. I will deal with that later.
Suddenly, after they thought their income tax returns had been accepted, going back three or four years, they would receive bills anywhere from $2,500 to $5,000. Many people could not afford to pay such bills. It put them practically into receivership on their farms. They never believed they were cheaters; however the assumption of the Department of National Revenue was that they were. I think they operated in a sneaky manner.
I am old enough to remember a lot of the James Cagney and Edward G. Robinson gangster movies. Even in the shoot-em-ups of the westerns we all used to love; when the crook was finally apprehended and hustled into headquarters to make a statement, the detective or the arresting officer always gave this warning, "Anything that you say can be held against you." That is part of American law. That is one of the disadvantages,
I guess, of being so close to our friend, the United States of America. We begin to assume that we have certain rights under Canadian or British law, or under common law, even judges rules, that we do not have. These traditional words of caution were never given to any of the people I have mentioned. I think they should have been warned of their legal rights if they were being investigated by an officer from National Revenue.
This situation goes back almost ten years. I guess it is not the turn of the hobby farmers now, perhaps it is the dentists, but I know whom they are bothering. They are bothering the people who are away from home who receive benefits for working away from home. A CPR trainman asked me what to do about his situation a little while ago.

But sizeable retroactive assessments cause severe problems to many of these people who are not tax dodgers, who are basically not tax cheaters but are operating under the assumptions that the income tax law allows them to make certain kinds of deductions. If they are not hauled into court, they are fooled into making statements which are later held against them.
When the inspectors come to them without any warning at all they ask for detailed advice. The average person does not have that kind of detailed accounting advice at his fingertips. I have never heard of these income tax officers or sleuths notifying people in advance that they are coming or what the nature of their visit is to be or that it would be a good idea, since the person is being investigated, to have his or her accountant or lawyer present. I have never heard of that happening yet, whether it is the small hobby farmer who is my constituent, a person who works away from home or whatever group that happens to be investigated at the moment in the spot check.
But I will say this much, that when the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) was minister of national revenue, I went to him about this problem. He made certain that the assessments did not go back more than one year. That was of great help. I do not know whether that continues to be policy, because I have not had the problem brought to me recently. But I can brag that through a combination of my efforts, the courtesy and willingness of the then minister of national revenue, we had some of the big sting taken out of the system.
Certainly the National Revenue Department should be looking for tax cheaters. I do not say that National Revenue should allow people to tip toe through the loopholes forever. I think if people are operating fraudulently, they should be nailed, and nailed as hard as they can be.
I mentioned other arms of government earlier that have resorted to what I consider to be sneaky practices as well. Working people who have had a long or a lengthy sickness or a jobless claim are frequently invited into the UIC offices for friendly chats, perhaps a little consultation and counselling. This cosy little arrangement purports to assist the claimant in finding new employment. There are no written questions. No one is invited to have his lawyer, his accountant, or his mother there to assist him. The person goes by himself and frequently condemns himself. We could be much more upright, honest, forthright and humane as a government department in dealing with people of whom 99 per cent are not crooks, cheaters or trying to get away with anything.
In the case of the UIC, once the interview is concluded the claimant is given a written document. He is expected then to sign it, and because he has signed certain things with certain words, he is probably, like many people before officialdom, frightened and embarrassed. He may even be degraded because he is idle. But the statement that is written up, not by the individual but by the counselling officer, is pretty close to what he thinks the story is, and he signs it just to get the hell out of there. He, too, like my friends the hobby farmer or the
Income Tax
CPR trainman, get a nice letter a few weeks later saying they are cut off or he owes this or that or something or other.
I suggest a lot can be done to improve the situation. We hear that people are cynical about government. They are certainly cynical about officialdom, bureaucrats and probably politicians too. But this practice only adds to that cynicism if this attitude prevails or is allowed to prevail.
My advice to people, and I have given it recently, in writing-I write it in my newspaper column-is that if they are visited by a bureaucrat who wants to know anything they should first insist on their rights. Before answering any questions they should make sure those questions are written questions. Demand your own professional assistance or have a witness with you. Request that you be allowed to take the questions home while you think about them, or get some advice about them, whether it is from UIC, National Revenue or some other department. Do not be hurried, pressured or intimidated into saying anything that does not reflect your case precisely and accurately.
What I say to people is: demand your own rights; do not be pushed around; do not be intimidated by any form of officialdom, no matter how heavy-handed it might be. If we can get people to learn to stand up for their own rights, they will feel better about themselves too. They will think a lot more of government and its agencies. It will teach government agencies to be less careless about the rights and feelings of individuals, for which the department was constructed to deal.
I am pleased that this topic has come forward. It has allowed me as a Member of Parliament to raise in a particular way some of my concerns that go back a decade. I am sure if they occurred then, they are continuing to occur, but until this point in time I have not had an opportunity to speak on them.
The hon. member for Chicoutimi said there was something like 91,000 reassessments last year. All I know is that when the hobby farmers were being investigated, I could not get the numbers being investigated. I was told that they were doing a number in British Columbia and a number in southern Ontario, but when I asked how many were being investigated in Quebec-because I am certain that many people live on small holdings and work in the woods part of the year, then there are those who work in town if they live on a small farm in New Brunswick-I was told that I could not have that information. I put the question on the Order Paper and I was told the information was not available. Therefore, if the hon. member for Chicoutimi was able to ferret out this information-he has it at least in total, perhaps not geographically-it would be very helpful, especially if a member feels that his constituents are being discriminated against while other people's constituents are allowed to go free in these spot checks.
That is about all I have to say. I congratulate the hon. member for Chicoutimi for bringing this matter forward. I hope that we will be able to discuss it further. If the resolution does not pass, I hope at least that the subject matter will be referred to the appropriate committee.

speechtext:
After I have concluded my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will reply to my hon. colleague. I suggest that it should be seen from the right perspective, failing which we would run the risk of setting a general rule on the basis of exceptions.
Mr. Speaker, as all hon. members are surely aware, the word "tax" is one which makes a great many shudder, but the reality of it is a necessity which affects nearly all Canadians. We must deal with it, therefore, in a co-operative spirit. The summary on auditing, I came across these last words: "One demonstrates co-operative spirit when one does with a smile what one must do anyway." I think that my hon. colleague possesses already this co-operative spirit, because he has made
remarks which contain elements of truth but which must be reconciled with the national revenue system.
Although by far the vast majority of Canadians are law-abiding citizens who are anxious to co-operate, a self-contributing tax system can exist only if there exists also a close scrutiny of income tax returns. The main purpose of taxauditing is to control the effectiveness of the self-contributing tax system. As such, it plays an important role in the realization of departmental objectives which are to collect taxes as prescribed by the act by encouraging compliance, and to ensure that Canadians have confidence in the integrity of the fiscal system.
Even in our most recent budget, we indicated that it was of paramount importance for our people to be convinced that we have an equitable tax system. And I suggest that through all the policies of the Department of National Revenue, we are doing our utmost to carry out this mandate. In the various taxation centres, tax returns are checked at the first stage of the process. District offices have set up programs to determine whether all applications for deductions are valid, to make sure that all revenues have been declared, and to identify the taxpayers who have not submitted an income tax return.
Let us consider now the Income Tax Act and the base system. The Canadian Income Tax system is a self-assessed tax system. Under this system, all corporations and persons, estates or taxable trusts must submit every year an income tax return on prescribed forms and determine the amounts which are payable for that year. After the initial processing and correction of obvious mistakes in filling out returns, and after the necessary cross-checking with returns from other people and information received from other sources, the return is selected for auditing and complete reviewing. Mr. Speaker, the examination is carried out under Section 231 of the Income Tax Act which compels all taxpayers to keep records and books necessary to determine the amount of income tax payable. Section 231 of the Act authorizes the Department to carry out this examination for any purposes related to the administration or enforcement of the act. In this regard, the act also authorizes the Department to seek and receive from any person information, records and accounts within such reasonable time as may be prescribed in the act. While the prospect of being subject to a tax audit is a strong motivation to voluntary compliance with the law, because, among other reasons, of the penalties applied in cases of obvious negligence or voluntary non-compliance, it still remains that the personal contact brought about by an audit is an ideal means of bringing home to the taxpayers the fact that each one of them only bears his legitimate part of the tax burden. It also helps, Mr. Speaker, to humanize a necessary tax-assessment system.
The type of audit made by taxation officers depends on the complexity of tax returns. There are two types: the office audit and the field audit. The office auditor usually works in the
March 26, 1982

district office where he is responsible for clarifying certain details about incomes, expenses and transactions reported by taxpayers. The auditor usually solves any problem through letters, telephone calls and personal interviews, while the field audit involves a detailed examination of the taxpayer's records. It usually occurs at his place of business and may take anywhere from a few days to several weeks to complete. Field auditors are professional accountants who are assigned the task of examining the complex records of large companies as well as the records of smaller companies made up of professional workers, such as farmers. These fields audits can take various other forms, including audits of a single industry and auditing teams. Audits of a whole industry involve the coordination of the audits carried out in a number of companies within one industry. The auditing teams include various specialists so that the records of large companies can be examined as thoroughly as possible. For instance, a data processing expert, a senior auditor and an economist on loan from another department may use their joint knowledge to audit a multinational which makes purchases outside Canada. This enables the department to make a more complete and more comprehensive audit. Since most large companies have computerized records, most major district offices now include computer science specialists.
The department also hires in its district offices corporate stock evaluators and real property assessors who determine the value of private company shares and of real estate. This evaluation is essential to determine capital gains. When the department makes an assessment and collects taxes, it ensures first of all that every taxpayer is treated fairly and impartially. That is why audits are reviewed in district offices. The main office co-ordinates and controls this review to guarantee that the tax legislation is applied consistently throughout the country. I have talked about the Income Tax Act and the system. I shall now deal, Mr. Speaker, with the audit philosophy and policy. I am well aware that this subject matter has an esoteric aspect, which means that it is incomprehensible to the layman. I would therefore like to explain the basic philosophy of the Department of National Revenue to the House.
Out of the 14.7 million taxpayers who filed income tax returns in 1979, a little under 10.5 million were employees and over 2.5 million were businessmen, salesmen on commission, farmers, self-employed fishermen, professionals or people who have an investment income. In addition, 550,000 companies file income tax returns. Most taxpayers receive wages or a salary from which taxes are deducted at the source. It is therefore relatively easy to check most tax returns with the information provided on salaries by the employers. We can therefore conclude that employees cause relatively few problems as far as complying with the law is concerned. Generally speaking, their taxes are collected through payroll deductions
Income Tax
and their incomes are readily verified by reference to information supplied by their employers. The obligation to keep books and records hardly applies to this group, and with the exception of certain cases where, for instance, expenses may be deducted from wages or salaries, audits are usually unnecessary. The department's audit program focuses mainly on the two and a half million self-employed workers and 550,000 corporations. The audit program is essentially based on seven broad guidelines used in preparing the program and in determining objectives for measuring compliance and estimating non-compliance. According to the guidelines, first of all, perfect compliance with the law is not and will never be attainable. Second, the most effective and least costly form of compliance is voluntary compliance. Third, tax recovery encourages voluntary compliance with the law. Fourth, recovery of taxes is theoretically feasible by doing a complete audit every four years. Here I should explain that in some cases the size and complexity of the taxpayer's business may, for reasons of practicality and maintaining good relations with such taxpayers, require more frequent audits covering periods of less than four years. Fifth, audit quality should be such that audit costs are in direct proportion to the resulting tax recovery. Sixth, each group of taxpayers should receive a minimum amount of auditing. Finally, establishing of categories of taxpayers for auditing purposes should be done in a rational and impartial manner.
The taxpayer has the assurance that the law will be enforced equally in all cases because of a spontaneous observance of the principle that taxpayers who pay what they owe should not be obliged to pay for the tax evasion perpetrated by others. In all fairness, the department has a responsibility to detect dishonest dealings and to take action against them. All groups of taxpayers must understand that the audit program is based on fair and impartial criteria. To do its job, our staff must be very ingenious and do a great deal of investigating.
Also, Mr. Speaker, the audit program is changed every year based on the resources allocated each district office. For reasons of optimum use of such limited resources, much care is taken in identifying groups of taxpayers or bodies that have to be looked at in priority and the choice of audit procedures which could lead to an improvement in tax compliance. Often a survey is made to assess the degree of compliance of a group of taxpayers that are not considered a category for programs purposes. Homogeneous groups are targeted, with the aim of eliminating practices that are gross violations of our tax acts. Homegeneity here is that of the tax base selected for audit purposes. For instance, some projects have dealt with matters as different as enumeration of surpluses, shareholder pension schemes, management fees, non-resident operations and the reuse of waste. If results of a project point to a special compliance problem, the scope of the project is widened to apply as need be throughout Canada. However, what exactly is an audit and what are the costs incurred? Quite often rumours spread concerning those being audited. This is akin to a visit to the

March 26, 1982
Income Tax
dentist. Although we know we are dealing with professionals there is anxiety in having a tooth pulled out, with all the accompanying pain. This is what happens in the actual case. The audit program is essentially based on the approximate number of returns filled by each group of taxpayers and the number of returns that can be audited by the available staff. Variations in the scope of an audit are influenced by the degree of non-compliance or the tax gap among various groups of taxpayers, as established as a result of former audit programs.
By auditing a random sample of returns in a particular group, and examining the tax collections from that sample, it is possible to project within certain parameters the probable tax collections for the whole group. This is one way of determining the monetary size and the scope of non-compliance that is often termed tax gap. Through periodical monitoring of the tax gap in a particular group of taxpayers based on audit procedures for that group, it is possible to assess the impact of an audit on tax compliance. There is an increase or a decrease in audit procedures depending on whether the tax gap has increased or decreased within this group. Additional data collected through these sample audits are processed by computer in order to find out trends that could be useful to the future retrieval of files for audit purposes.
As audits are done in 28 district offices, the department wishes to ensure that the act is interpreted and administered in
a consistent manner. That is the main purpose of the audit review system which includes district offices and the Head Office. Every district office has a review unit which is responsible for achieving this goal within the district boundaries, whereas the operational audit division of the head office is responsible for ensuring consistency throughout the country. Since the main purpose of a tax audit is to control and maintain the self-assessment system, let me elaborate on it a little. As I mentioned at the outset, there are two kinds of audit, the office audit and the field audit, the latter being the main tool available to the department to administer the act. A field audit can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks depending on the nature of the operations.
